chapters.title: Email, explained
chapters.intro:
How email actually works, why mail servers are so easy to get wrong, what fifty years of fixes have solved, and what is still broken. Written for anyone who has tried to run a mail server, or wondered why it is so hard.

It is the guide we wished we had when we were learning. It is written to be useful whatever server you run; REST Mail's own approach comes last in each chapter, after the problem and the standard fixes, never instead of them.

sections.title: How to read it
sections.html:
Each chapter follows the same pattern:

  1. The problem. What goes wrong without this, in plain words.
  2. How it works. The protocol or setting, with a diagram.
  3. What goes wrong. The common mistakes, and why they are easy to make.
  4. How REST Mail handles it. With links to the code that does it.
  5. Sources. The RFCs and documentation every claim comes from.

These files are the source of truth. The guide on rest-mail.com is built from them, with the diagrams made interactive, so the two never drift apart. How that build works is being designed in docs/design/email-explained-website.md.

chapters.title: The journey of a message
chapters.part: How email works
chapters.summary: What happens between pressing Send and the message arriving, hop by hop, and who is responsible for it at each step.
chapters.intro:
Alice, at alice@example.com, writes to Bob, at bob@example.org, and presses Send. A second later the message is in Bob's inbox. In between, it has passed through at least four programs on two or more servers, run by two different organisations that have never heard of each other, using a protocol older than the web.

This chapter follows that message hop by hop. Each later chapter takes one of these hops, or one of the protections around them, and explains it in depth.

The diagram's source is journey.workflow.json.

sections.title: The cast
sections.html:
Email is not one program. The standard description of the internet's mail architecture, RFC 5598, names the roles a message passes through. A single server often plays several of them, but the roles stay distinct:

  • The mail user agent (MUA) is the mail app: Thunderbird, Apple Mail, Outlook, a phone's mail app, or webmail in a browser. It is where a message is written and read.
  • The mail submission agent (MSA) takes new mail from a user's own app. It asks the user to sign in, so it knows who is sending.
  • The mail transfer agent (MTA) moves mail between servers. Postfix, Exim and Sendmail are MTAs. The server that receives mail for a domain is that domain's MX, after the DNS record that names it.
  • The mail delivery agent (MDA) puts a message into the right mailbox, and is where filtering rules run.
  • The message store holds mailboxes, and serves them to mail apps over IMAP, POP3 or JMAP. Dovecot is a message store.

sections.title: Hop by hop
sections.html:
1. Submission: Alice's app hands the message over

Alice's mail app connects to her provider's submission server and signs in. The standard ports are 587 (RFC 6409), where the connection starts unencrypted and is upgraded with STARTTLS, and 465, where it is encrypted from the first byte. Since 2018, RFC 8314 has recommended 465. Signing in is what lets the server send to any address in the world for Alice, and refuse to do so for a stranger. Who may send explains how.

The app speaks SMTP, the same protocol servers use between themselves: MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, then the message. SMTP as a conversation goes through it line by line.

2. The sending server queues it

Alice's server answers 250 OK and puts the message in a queue. From here on, Alice's app is no longer involved: she can close her laptop. Before the message leaves, the server usually signs it with DKIM, so that Bob's server can check it really came from example.com (DKIM).

3. Finding Bob's server

Alice's server asks the DNS for the MX records of example.org: the names of the servers that accept its mail, each with a preference number. It tries the lowest number first, and moves on to the next if that one does not answer (RFC 5321 §5.1). DNS for email covers the details, including what happens when a domain has no MX at all.

4. Server to server, on port 25

Alice's server connects to Bob's MX on port 25 and speaks SMTP again. This time there is no sign-in: Bob's server accepts mail from anyone in the world, but only for its own users. It upgrades the connection with STARTTLS if both sides can, which is not guaranteed (Encryption in transit).

If Bob's server is down, or answers "try again later", the message stays in Alice's server's queue, and is retried for days before it gives up and sends Alice a bounce (Bounces, queues and retries).

5. Bob's server decides whether to accept it

Before it says yes, Bob's server checks what it can:

  • Is the connecting address on a blocklist? (Spam defences)
  • Is the sending server allowed to send for example.com? (SPF)
  • Is the DKIM signature valid? (DKIM)
  • Does example.com ask for failures to be rejected? (DMARC)
  • Does the content look like spam or carry a virus?

Then it answers 250 OK to the message. That reply matters more than it looks. RFC 5321 §6.1 says that by sending it, the receiver "is accepting responsibility for delivering or relaying the message". From now on, if the message is lost, it is Bob's server's fault, not Alice's. The black hole is about what happens when a server takes that responsibility and then drops the message.

6. Delivery into Bob's mailbox

Bob's MTA hands the message to the delivery agent, often over LMTP (RFC 2033), a local cousin of SMTP. Bob's own filtering rules run here, usually written in Sieve: file mail from this list in that folder, reply with "I'm on holiday".

7. Bob reads it

Bob's mail app fetches the message from the message store over IMAP, POP3 or JMAP. IMAP keeps the mail on the server and in sync across devices; POP3 usually downloads and removes it; JMAP is the modern, HTTP-based successor (Reading mail).

sections.title: Every hop leaves a trace
sections.html:
Each server that handles the message adds a Received: line at the top of its header: who it came from, who received it, when, and how. RFC 5321 makes this a requirement: a server "MUST insert trace ("time stamp" or "Received") information at the beginning of the message content" (§4.4).

Read from the bottom up, those lines are the message's journey. They are the first thing to look at when a message is late, or marked as spam. Most mail apps show them under "Show original" or "View source".

sections.title: Three things to take away
sections.html:
• There are two kinds of SMTP connection. A user's app submits mail with a password, and may send anywhere. A server delivers mail without one, and may only deliver for the receiving server's own users. Mixing them up is the open relay.
  • Responsibility moves with the 250 after the message. Until then, the sender's server must keep trying. After it, the receiver must deliver or bounce.
  • Nothing in the original protocol proves who sent a message. SPF, DKIM and DMARC were added on top, decades later. Part 2 of this guide goes through them one at a time.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
REST Mail plays every role in the cast, in one server, behind one REST API:

  • Submission is on port 465 only, encrypted from the first byte, and requires a sign-in. There is no cleartext submission port to configure: the setting for 587 does not exist (internal/gateway/smtp/server.go, ListenAndServe; internal/config/config.go).
  • Port 25 accepts mail from other servers, for REST Mail's own mailboxes only (session.go, Rcpt).
  • Checks before accepting run as a per-domain pipeline of filters: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ARC, greylisting, spam and virus scanning (internal/pipeline/filters/).
  • The queue retries delivery and bounces what it cannot deliver (internal/gateway/queue/worker.go). To another REST Mail server, it can deliver over HTTPS instead of SMTP (RESTMAIL).
  • Reading is over IMAP on 993 and POP3 on 995, both encrypted from the first byte, or directly through the REST API, which REST Mail's own apps use.
  • Trace lines: each reception adds a Received: line, recording whether the connection was encrypted and signed in (ESMTPS, ESMTPSA), and naming the recipient only when there is exactly one, so a Bcc recipient is never revealed to the others (received.go).

chapters.title: DNS for email
chapters.part: How email works
chapters.summary: How a server finds where to deliver mail, the records every mail domain publishes, and the DNS mistakes that send mail nowhere.
chapters.intro:
An email address names a person and a domain, never a server. bob@example.org says nothing about which machine takes Bob's mail. That answer lives in the DNS, the internet's directory. So does almost everything else a mail server needs to know about a domain: who may send for it, where its signing keys are, and what to do with mail that fails its checks.

Get the DNS right and mail flows. Get one record wrong and mail goes to the wrong place, or nowhere, often without an error anyone sees.

The diagram's source is dns.workflow.json.

sections.title: MX: where mail for a domain goes
sections.titleHtml: MX: where mail for a domain goes
sections.html:
An MX record ("mail exchanger") names a server that accepts mail for the domain, with a preference number:

example.org.   3600  IN  MX  10  mx1.example.org.
example.org.   3600  IN  MX  20  mx2.example.org.

A sending server sorts the records by preference and tries the lowest number first. Records with the same number must be tried in random order, to spread the load. If the first server cannot be reached, the next is tried, and a sender "SHOULD try at least two addresses" (RFC 5321 §5.1).

Two rules about the name an MX points to:

  • It must be a host name with an address record (A or AAAA), not an IP address. RFC 5321 requires the answer to "contain a domain name", which "MUST return at least one address record".
  • It must not be an alias (CNAME). "The domain name used as [...] part of the value of a MX resource record must not be an alias" (RFC 2181 §10.3). Many servers follow one anyway, but not all do.

sections.title: When there is no MX
sections.html:
RFC 5321 gives three different answers three different meanings:

The DNS says Meaning What the sender must do
The domain does not exist (NXDOMAIN) A typo, or a domain that has gone Report an error, at once
A temporary failure The DNS could not answer now Queue the message and retry later
The domain exists, with no MX An old-style domain Deliver to the domain's own address (A or AAAA), the implicit MX

The implicit MX is a leftover from before MX records existed. It means any domain with a web server's address seems, to a sending server, to accept mail. Mail for info@www.example.com is delivered to the web server, which usually refuses the connection, so the message sits in queues for days before it bounces.

sections.title: Null MX: "this domain takes no mail"
sections.titleHtml: Null MX: "this domain takes no mail"
sections.html:
A domain that never receives mail can say so with a null MX (RFC 7505):

www.example.com.  3600  IN  MX  0  .

The . is not a host. It means there is no mail exchanger. A sending server that sees it fails the message straight away, with 556 5.1.10, instead of retrying for days. RFC 7505 says what that buys: "Null MX allows a mail system to report the delivery failure when the user sends the message, rather than hours or days later", and it lets the bounces of forged spam be "disposed of efficiently".

Do not publish a null MX for a domain you send from: receivers may reject your mail, because a reply would have nowhere to go. For a domain that also sends nothing, add an SPF record of v=spf1 -all.

sections.title: A, AAAA and reverse DNS
sections.html:
• A and AAAA records give the MX host's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
  • Reverse DNS maps an address back to a name, with a PTR record. It is set by whoever owns the address: your hosting provider or ISP, not your domain's DNS host.

Receiving servers check that the connecting address has a PTR record, and that the name it gives resolves back to the same address ("forward-confirmed reverse DNS"). Gmail requires it of everyone who sends to it: sending domains and addresses must have "valid forward and reverse DNS records, also referred to as PTR records" (Google, Email sender guidelines). A missing PTR record is one of the most common reasons a new server's mail is rejected while everything else checks out.

sections.title: The records that carry policy
sections.html:
Everything added to email since the 1990s is published in the DNS, mostly as TXT records under well-known names. Each has a chapter of its own:

Record Name What it says Chapter
SPF example.org TXT Which servers may send for the domain SPF
DKIM key <selector>._domainkey.example.org TXT The public key that checks signatures DKIM
DMARC _dmarc.example.org TXT What to do with mail that fails, and where to send reports DMARC
MTA-STS _mta-sts.example.org TXT That a TLS policy is published over HTTPS MTA-STS and DANE
TLS-RPT _smtp._tls.example.org TXT Where to send reports of TLS failures MTA-STS and DANE
TLSA _25._tcp.mx1.example.org TLSA The MX's certificate, signed with DNSSEC (DANE) MTA-STS and DANE
SRV _imaps._tcp.example.org and others Where mail apps connect Finding the server

Two rules catch people out. A domain must have only one SPF record: two make SPF fail with an error for every message (RFC 7208 §3.2). And each of these names is exact: a DMARC record at dmarc.example.org, without the underscore, is simply not found.

sections.title: Changes take time
sections.html: Every record has a TTL ("time to live"): how many seconds other servers may keep a copy before asking again. A change is seen by everyone only once the old copies have expired. Before moving mail to a new server, lower the TTL of the MX and address records a day or more ahead, so the switch takes minutes rather than hours. Migrating step by step does this in order.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• The MX points at the wrong host after a move, or at a name with no A record. Mail queues on senders' servers for days, then bounces.
  • The MX points at a CNAME, which some servers follow and others refuse.
  • No PTR record, or one left at the provider's default name. Large providers reject or junk the mail.
  • Two SPF records, often one added by each service the domain uses. SPF fails for everything.
  • A record in the wrong place: at dmarc. instead of _dmarc., or with the domain repeated by a DNS host that appends it (_dmarc.example.org.example.org).
  • A long TTL during a migration, so half the internet still delivers to the old server.

sections.title: How to check your own domain
sections.titleHtml: How to check your own domain
sections.html:
dig +short MX example.org                 # where mail goes, with preferences
dig +short A mx1.example.org              # the MX host's address
dig +short -x 203.0.113.25                # its reverse DNS (PTR)
dig +short TXT example.org                # SPF (look for exactly one v=spf1)
dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.org         # DMARC

The PTR should name the MX host, and that name's A record should be the same address.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• It prints the records a domain needs, and checks them. For each domain, chore dns:show lists the mail host's A record, the MX, an SPF record (v=spf1 mx -all, naming the MX rather than an address, so moving the server changes one A record), a DMARC record at the domain's own policy (p=none until an admin raises it), the DKIM key, and the PTR to ask the address's owner for. chore dns:check compares them with what is published (internal/dns/mail_records.go).
  • The server never configures its own public address. It comes from wherever the server is exposed, so records that need it are left out rather than guessed.
  • Null MX is honoured: mail to a domain with MX 0 . fails at once with 556 5.1.10, as RFC 7505 asks (internal/gateway/queue/worker.go).
  • Implicit MX is used for a domain without MX records. Today REST Mail cannot tell that case from a domain that does not exist, so mail to a misspelled domain is retried until it expires. Fixing that, as RFC 5321 requires, is #713.
  • International domain names are looked up in their ASCII form (xn--…), while the queue keeps the Unicode form for display (#153).
  • SRV records for mail apps are not yet in the printed set, and the list in the code names ports REST Mail does not listen on. Both are #712.

chapters.title: SMTP as a conversation
chapters.part: How email works
chapters.summary: The commands and replies two mail servers exchange, line by line, what the reply codes mean, and how to hold the conversation yourself.
chapters.intro:
SMTP, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, is how every email moves between servers, and from a mail app to its own server. It was first published in 1982 (RFC 821). Today's version is RFC 5321, from 2008, and it is still a conversation in plain text: one side sends a command, the other answers with a number and a sentence.

That is good news for anyone running a mail server. Every log line, every bounce and every error message is a piece of this conversation. Once you can read it, you can tell where a message stopped, and why.

The diagram's source is smtp.sequence.json.

sections.title: A whole conversation
sections.html:
Here is one message delivered from mail.example.com to mx.example.org. The client's lines are marked C: and the server's S:.

S: 220 mx.example.org ESMTP ready
C: EHLO mail.example.com
S: 250-mx.example.org Hello mail.example.com
S: 250-SIZE 52428800
S: 250-8BITMIME
S: 250-PIPELINING
S: 250-STARTTLS
S: 250 ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES
C: STARTTLS
S: 220 2.0.0 Ready to start TLS
   (the TLS handshake; everything after it is encrypted)
C: EHLO mail.example.com
S: 250-mx.example.org Hello mail.example.com
S: 250 ...
C: MAIL FROM:<alice@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.0 OK
C: RCPT TO:<bob@example.org>
S: 250 2.1.5 OK
C: DATA
S: 354 Start mail input; end with <CRLF>.<CRLF>
C: From: Alice <alice@example.com>
C: To: Bob <bob@example.org>
C: Subject: Lunch?
C: Date: Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:00:00 +0000
C: Message-ID: <1234@example.com>
C:
C: Are you free on Tuesday?
C: .
S: 250 2.0.0 OK queued as 7F3A1
C: QUIT
S: 221 2.0.0 Bye

sections.title: The commands
sections.html:
• EHLO ("extended hello") opens the conversation and names the client. The server answers with the extensions it supports, one per line. The old HELO does the same without extensions (RFC 5321 §4.1.1.1).
  • STARTTLS upgrades the connection to an encrypted one, after which the client starts again with EHLO (RFC 3207). Why that upgrade can be stripped by an attacker is in Encryption in transit.
  • AUTH signs in, on a submission port (RFC 4954; see Who may send).
  • MAIL FROM starts a message and gives the envelope sender: where bounces go. It is often different from the From: line the reader sees (The message itself).
  • RCPT TO gives one recipient. A message for three people has three RCPT TO lines, and the server answers each one separately.
  • DATA sends the message itself: header lines, a blank line, then the body. It ends with a line holding a single dot. A body line that really starts with a dot gets a second one added, which the server removes ("dot-stuffing", §4.5.2).
  • RSET abandons the current message, NOOP does nothing (useful to keep a connection alive), and QUIT ends the conversation.
  • VRFY and EXPN ask whether an address exists, or what a list expands to. Most servers disable them, because they hand spammers a list of real addresses; RFC 5321 allows that (§7.3).

sections.title: Reading the replies
sections.html:
Every reply starts with three digits. The first one says what kind of answer it is (RFC 5321 §4.2.1):

First digit Meaning What the client does
2 Done Carries on
3 Go on, send more Sends the message data
4 Failed for now Keeps the message, and tries again later
5 Failed for good Gives up, and sends a bounce

The difference between 4 and 5 decides whether a message is retried for days or bounced at once. Getting it wrong either way hurts: a 4 for a mailbox that will never exist fills queues, and a 5 for a passing problem loses mail.

Most servers add an enhanced status code after the number, such as 5.1.1. Its three parts give the class (2, 4 or 5 again), the subject (1 addressing, 2 mailbox, 3 mail system, 4 network, 5 protocol, 6 content, 7 security) and the detail (RFC 3463, announced by ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES, RFC 2034).

The replies you will meet most often:

Reply Meaning
220 Ready (the greeting, and the go-ahead for STARTTLS)
221 Closing the connection
250 OK
354 Send the message data
421 Service not available now; try later
450 / 451 Not now: mailbox busy, greylisted, local error
452 Not now: out of storage, or too many recipients
454 4.7.1 Not now: often "Relay access denied" (Postfix's default)
530 5.7.0 Sign in first
535 5.7.8 Sign-in failed
550 5.1.1 No such mailbox
550 5.7.1 Refused by policy: blocklisted, failed DMARC, not allowed to relay
552 Message too big, or mailbox full
554 Transaction failed
556 5.1.10 The domain accepts no mail (null MX)

The sentence after the code is for people, and servers put useful detail there: which blocklist listed you, which DMARC policy failed. Read it.

sections.title: Extensions
sections.html:
EHLO's answer lists what the server can do beyond the 1982 basics. Each was added by an RFC of its own:

Extension What it adds Standard
SIZE The largest message accepted, so a client need not send a huge one only to be refused RFC 1870
8BITMIME Message bodies with bytes above 127, not only 7-bit ASCII RFC 6152
PIPELINING Several commands sent without waiting for each reply RFC 2920
STARTTLS Upgrade to an encrypted connection RFC 3207
AUTH Sign in RFC 4954
ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES The x.y.z codes RFC 2034
CHUNKING BDAT: the message sent in counted chunks, with no dot-stuffing RFC 3030
SMTPUTF8 Addresses and headers in any script, such as 用户@例子.广告 RFC 6531
DSN Ask for a delivery report, success or failure RFC 3461
REQUIRETLS This message may only travel encrypted RFC 8689
LIMITS The server's limits, such as recipients per message RFC 9422

sections.title: Hold the conversation yourself
sections.html:
Talking to a server by hand is the quickest way to see what it does. Port 25 on most servers upgrades with STARTTLS:

openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect mx.example.org:25 -crlf

Then type EHLO test.example, and read the extensions. To send a test message with less typing, swaks holds the whole conversation and prints it:

swaks --server mx.example.org --to postmaster@example.org

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• Line endings. SMTP lines end with carriage return and line feed (CRLF). Some servers have long also accepted a bare line feed. In December 2023, SEC Consult showed that two servers which disagree about where a message ends can be made to accept a second, forged message hidden inside the first: SMTP smuggling (SEC Consult, 2023). Postfix's author explains the fixes Postfix shipped, and why the bare line feed was accepted in the first place, in SMTP Smuggling.
  • A 4 that should be a 5, or the reverse. See the table above.
  • A greeting that lies. A server's EHLO name should be its real host name, with matching DNS. Many receivers score or refuse clients whose EHLO does not resolve.
  • Talking before the greeting. A client that sends commands before the server's 220 is almost always a spam bot. Postfix's postscreen waits a few seconds to catch exactly that (POSTSCREEN_README).

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
REST Mail's SMTP is rest-mail/go-smtp, a fork of emersion/go-smtp, with a test for each RFC it implements. The gateway configures it in internal/gateway/smtp/server.go:

  • Extensions advertised: PIPELINING, 8BITMIME, ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES, CHUNKING, SMTPUTF8, SIZE, LIMITS RCPTMAX=100, STARTTLS on port 25, AUTH only on an encrypted submission connection, and RESTMAIL, its own extension for delivery over HTTPS (RESTMAIL).
  • Only CRLF ends a line. A command ended by a bare line feed is refused with 500 5.5.2 and the connection is closed. Only <CR><LF>.<CR><LF> ends a message, which is what SMTP smuggling relies on servers getting wrong.
  • The server waits at least 5 minutes for the next command, as RFC 5321 asks, and a message that is still arriving at a reasonable rate is never cut off for being large (transfer_rate.go).
  • As a client, delivering to other servers, REST Mail today times each attempt as a whole, where RFC 5321 asks for a timeout per command, with 5 minutes for the greeting and 10 for the final reply. Changing that is #714.

chapters.title: The message itself
chapters.part: How email works
chapters.summary: What an email is made of: the envelope that routes it, the header the reader sees, and the MIME parts that carry text, HTML and attachments.
chapters.intro:
An email is a text file. Open one with "Show original" in any mail app and you see it: lines of Name: value at the top, a blank line, then the body. Everything else, the formatting, the pictures, the attachments, the non-English text, is encoded into that text, because the system it travels through was built for 7-bit ASCII in 1982 and has had to stay compatible ever since.

There is also a part you never see in that file: the envelope, which decides where the message actually goes.

The diagram's source is message.tree.json.

sections.title: The envelope and the header are different things
sections.titleHtml: The envelope and the header are different things
sections.html:
Think of a paper letter. The address on the envelope is what the postal service reads. The letter inside has its own "Dear Bob" and "From Alice", which only the reader sees. They usually agree. Nothing makes them.

Email works the same way:

The envelope The header
What it is The SMTP commands MAIL FROM and RCPT TO (SMTP) The From:, To:, Cc: lines inside the message
Who reads it Mail servers, to route the message The reader's mail app, to display it
Defined by RFC 5321 RFC 5322
The sender MAIL FROM: where bounces go, also called the return path From:: the author
The recipients One RCPT TO per recipient, Bcc included To: and Cc:, never Bcc

Two consequences matter every day:

  • Bcc works because of the envelope. A Bcc recipient gets a RCPT TO, and appears nowhere in the header. A mail app or server that leaves a Bcc: line in the message it sends reveals who was copied.
  • The From: line can say anything. Nothing in SMTP checks it against the envelope, or against who connected. That is why phishing works, and why DMARC exists: it is the first standard to check the From: line the reader actually sees.

When the message is finally delivered, the server records the envelope sender in a Return-Path: header line, so the reader can see where bounces would have gone (RFC 5321 §4.4).

sections.title: The header
sections.html:
Each header line is a field name, a colon, and a value. RFC 5322 requires only two of them: "The only required header fields are the origination date field and the originator address field(s)" (§3.6), which are Date: and From:. Every message should also have a Message-ID:, a unique name used to thread replies (In-Reply-To:, References:).

Others are added along the way:

  • Received:, one per server the message passed through, newest first (The journey of a message).
  • DKIM-Signature:, the sender's signature (DKIM).
  • Authentication-Results:, the receiving server's verdict on SPF, DKIM and DMARC (RFC 8601).
  • List-Unsubscribe: on mailing lists and newsletters (Bulk mail).

A header line may not be longer than 998 characters, and should be no longer than 78; a long value is "folded" onto the next line, which starts with a space (RFC 5322 §2.1.1).

sections.title: Text that is not ASCII
sections.html:
The original format allowed only ASCII. Two ways around that exist:

  • Encoded words (RFC 2047) wrap non-ASCII header text in an ASCII disguise: Subject: =?UTF-8?B?Q2Fmw6k=?= is "Café".
  • SMTPUTF8 (RFC 6531, RFC 6532) lets UTF-8 appear directly in headers and addresses, between servers that both announce it. It is what makes an address like 用户@例子.广告 possible.

sections.title: MIME: one message, many parts
sections.html:
MIME (RFC 2045 to RFC 2049) turns a body into a tree of parts. Each part has its own small header saying what it is (Content-Type:) and how it is encoded for the trip (Content-Transfer-Encoding:). A typical message with an HTML body and an attachment looks like this, shortened:

From: Alice <alice@example.com>
To: Bob <bob@example.org>
Subject: The report
Date: Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:00:00 +0000
Message-ID: <5678@example.com>
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="outer"

--outer
Content-Type: multipart/alternative; boundary="inner"

--inner
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8
Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable

Here is the report. Caf=C3=A9 on Tuesday?
--inner
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

<p>Here is the report. Café on Tuesday?</p>
--inner--
--outer
Content-Type: application/pdf; name="report.pdf"
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="report.pdf"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64

JVBERi0xLjcKJcfsj6IKNSAwIG9iago8PC9MZW5ndGggNiAwIFI...
--outer--
  • multipart/mixed holds parts that belong together: the message and its attachments.
  • multipart/alternative holds the same content in several forms, plainest first. A mail app shows the last one it can display: the "best choice is the LAST part of a type supported by the recipient" (RFC 2046 §5.1.4).
  • The boundary is a string that marks where each part starts and ends. It must not appear inside any part.
  • Content-Disposition says whether a part is shown inline or offered as an attachment (RFC 2183).

sections.title: The encodings
sections.html:
Encoding What it is for Cost
7bit Plain ASCII text, short lines None
8bit Text with non-ASCII bytes, to servers that announce 8BITMIME None
quoted-printable Mostly-ASCII text with some accented letters: é becomes =C3=A9 Small, for mostly-ASCII text
base64 Anything binary: images, PDFs, archives A third bigger: 3 bytes become 4 characters

The base64 cost is why a 15 MB attachment can hit a 20 MB message limit: once encoded, it is about 20 MB.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• A Bcc: line left in the sent message, revealing who was copied.
  • Missing Date: or Message-ID:. Gmail requires every sender to format messages "according to the Internet Message Format standard, RFC 5322" (Google), and spam filters score malformed headers.
  • Changing a message in transit. A mailing list that adds a footer or a [list] tag to the subject changes signed content, and breaks the DKIM signature (DKIM, ARC).
  • HTML only. A message with no plain text alternative is harder to read for some readers, and scores worse with some filters.
  • Size limits after encoding. An attachment that fits the limit as a file may not fit once base64 has grown it by a third.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• MIME is parsed with emersion/go-message, into the parts the REST API returns: text, HTML, attachments and inline images (internal/mime/).
  • Bcc is stripped from every message before it is relayed, once, in the same place it is DKIM-signed, so no send path can forget (internal/outbound/prepare.go, #171).
  • Header checks are a pipeline filter: by default it requires From: and Date:, and rejects header injection; requiring Message-ID: is a setting (header_validate.go).
  • Message-IDs REST Mail creates are random and unique, in the sender's domain (internal/mail/messageid.go).
  • UTF-8 throughout. REST Mail accepts SMTPUTF8, and for an IMAP or POP3 app that has not asked for UTF-8 it rewrites the header into ASCII encoded words, as RFC 6855 to RFC 6858 describe, leaving the body untouched (internal/gateway/rawmsg/downgrade.go).

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• RFC 5322: Internet Message Format.
  • RFC 5321 §4.4: trace fields and Return-Path.
  • MIME: RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2049, RFC 2183.
  • Internationalised email: RFC 6531, RFC 6532, RFC 6855, RFC 6856.
  • RFC 8601: Authentication-Results.
  • Google: Email sender guidelines.
  • REST Mail: internal/mime/, internal/outbound/, internal/gateway/rawmsg/.

chapters.title: Bounces, queues and retries
chapters.part: How email works
chapters.summary: What a mail server does when delivery fails: how long it keeps trying, how it tells the sender, and how bounces themselves become abuse.
chapters.intro:
Email is not instant, and was never meant to be. When Bob's server is down, busy, or not sure about a message yet, Alice's server does not give up. It keeps the message in its queue and tries again, for days. Only when it is sure the message cannot be delivered does it send Alice a bounce: a message explaining what went wrong.

That patience is one of email's great strengths. It also needs rules, because a server that gives up too soon loses mail, one that never gives up fills its disk, and one that sends bounces carelessly floods innocent people with them.

The diagram's source is queue.lifecycle.json.

sections.title: For now, or for good
sections.html:
Every attempt ends with a reply from the receiving server, and its first digit decides what happens next (SMTP as a conversation):

  • 2xx: delivered. The message leaves the queue.
  • 4xx: a temporary failure. The receiver is busy, greylisting, short of disk, or could not check something. The message stays queued and is tried again later.
  • 5xx: a permanent failure. No such mailbox, refused by policy, message too big. The sender is told at once.
  • No reply at all: the connection failed or timed out. Treated as temporary.

sections.title: How long to keep trying
sections.html:
RFC 5321 §4.5.4.1 sets the expectations:

In general, the retry interval SHOULD be at least 30 minutes; however, more sophisticated and variable strategies will be beneficial when the SMTP client can determine the reason for non-delivery.

Retries continue until the message is transmitted or the sender gives up; the give-up time generally needs to be at least 4-5 days.

Postfix, for example, waits at least 5 minutes between attempts and at most 4000 seconds (about 67 minutes), and gives up after 5 days (postconf(5): minimal_backoff_time = 300s, maximal_backoff_time = 4000s, maximal_queue_lifetime = 5d).

Five days covers the ordinary disasters: a server down over a long weekend, a DNS mistake fixed on Monday, a full mailbox emptied after a holiday.

sections.title: The bounce
sections.html:
When a message cannot be delivered, the server sends a delivery status notification (DSN) to the envelope sender, the MAIL FROM address (The message itself). Its format is standard (RFC 3464): a multipart/report (RFC 6522) with three parts.

  1. A text explanation for the person.
  2. A machine-readable part, message/delivery-status, that programs can act on:
    Reporting-MTA: dns; mail.example.com
Final-Recipient: rfc822; bob@example.org
Action: failed
Status: 5.1.1
Remote-MTA: dns; mx.example.org
Diagnostic-Code: smtp; 550 5.1.1 <bob@example.org>: no such user
  3. The original message, or its header.

Two rules keep bounces from making things worse:

  • A bounce is sent with an empty envelope sender, MAIL FROM:<>. So if the bounce itself cannot be delivered, nothing bounces back: "if this address is null ("<>"), the receiver-SMTP MUST NOT send a notification" (RFC 5321 §6.1).
  • Once a server has said 250, it must deliver or bounce. It "MUST NOT lose the message for frivolous reasons", and "If there is a delivery failure after acceptance of a message, the receiver-SMTP MUST formulate and mail a notification message" (the same section). Silently dropping accepted mail is the black hole.

A sender can ask for more with the DSN extension (RFC 3461): NOTIFY=SUCCESS for a report when delivery succeeds, NOTIFY=DELAY for a warning while it is still queued, or NOTIFY=NEVER for none.

sections.title: Refuse, don't bounce
sections.html:
There are two ways to say no to a message for a mailbox that does not exist:

  • Refuse it during the conversation, with 550 5.1.1 to RCPT TO. The sending server keeps the message and writes the bounce to its own user, who is real, because they had to sign in to send.
  • Accept it, then bounce it. Now your server writes a bounce to whatever MAIL FROM the sender claimed. Spam forges that address. Your bounces land on an innocent person, by the thousand.

The second is called backscatter. Postfix's documentation describes it from the victim's side: "When a spammer or worm sends mail with forged sender addresses, innocent sites are flooded with undeliverable mail notifications" (BACKSCATTER_README). The cure is to decide during the conversation: know your recipients at RCPT TO, and reject spam and viruses before the final 250, not after.

sections.title: Automatic replies
sections.html:
Vacation messages and other auto-replies are bounces' cousins, with the same risks, and a standard of their own (RFC 3834):

  • Mark them with Auto-Submitted: auto-replied, so other responders do not answer back.
  • Never reply to <>. "Responders MUST NOT generate any response for which the destination of that response would be a null address" (§2).
  • Reply once per sender per period, not to every message. Sieve's vacation extension defaults to 7 days (RFC 5230).
  • Send them with an empty envelope sender too (RFC 5230 §5.1).

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• A queue full of spam bounces, the first visible sign of an open relay.
  • Backscatter, from accepting first and checking later.
  • 5xx for a temporary problem, such as a DNS lookup that timed out at the receiver: real mail bounces that a retry would have delivered.
  • 4xx for a permanent one: mail to an address that will never exist sits in queues for days before the sender hears.
  • Giving up too soon, before the 4–5 days RFC 5321 expects.
  • Accepted, then dropped: a filter that discards mail it has already said yes to, with no bounce.
  • Auto-reply loops between two responders that do not mark their mail.

sections.title: Look at your own queue
sections.html:
• Postfix: postqueue -p lists the queue with each message's last error; postqueue -f retries everything now; postcat -q <id> shows one message.
  • Exim: exim -bp lists it; exim -Mvh <id> shows a message's header.

A queue that keeps growing is a symptom, never the problem: read the errors.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Retries by reason. The queue classifies each failure and retries on a schedule for that reason, which is the "more sophisticated" strategy RFC 5321 allows: greylisting is retried after 7 minutes, a remote asking it to slow down after 15, a full mailbox after an hour, a TLS problem after 15 minutes, a DNS failure after 5, and a failed connection or anything else after 5, as Postfix's minimal_backoff_time. Each wait doubles, up to 4 hours, with random jitter of a fifth either way so that messages held up by the same outage do not all retry at once (internal/gateway/queue/retry.go).
  • How long: REST Mail retries for 5 days before it bounces, whatever the reason, a full mailbox included, within RFC 5321's 4–5 days and as Postfix's maximal_queue_lifetime. The retry budget, 60 attempts, outlasts every schedule, so the deadline is what ends retrying (internal/db/models/queue.go, QueueLifetime, #711).
  • Bounces are RFC 3464 reports, marked Auto-Submitted: auto-generated, with Remote-MTA and Last-Attempt-Date, and with every remote value cleaned so a hostile reply cannot inject header lines (worker.go, buildDSNMessage).
  • Bounces go only where they belong. A bounce is written straight into the sender's own inbox, only if the queued message really came from that mailbox, and no more than a set number per mailbox per hour, so a forged sender cannot be used to flood someone with bounces.
  • No backscatter from port 25. REST Mail refuses an unknown recipient with 550 5.1.1 during the conversation, and runs its checks before it answers the message, so it does not accept mail and bounce it later.
  • Bounces for senders elsewhere. When a forward to another server fails for good, the original sender is told by mail: a DSN with a null reverse path, queued like any outbound message and limited per recipient as a local bounce is (#715).
  • Not yet compliant: the vacation responder can answer a bounce and sends from the user's address rather than <> (#716).
  • Hard bounces are remembered. An address that bounces with "no such mailbox" is suppressed for 90 days, so REST Mail does not keep sending to it (suppression.go, #141).

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• RFC 5321: §4.5.4.1 (retries), §6.1 (reliable delivery and notifications).
  • RFC 3461: the DSN extension. RFC 3464: the DSN format. RFC 6522: multipart/report.
  • RFC 3834: automatic responses. RFC 5230: the Sieve vacation extension.
  • Postfix: postconf(5), BACKSCATTER_README.
  • REST Mail: internal/gateway/queue/, internal/pipeline/filters/vacation.go.

chapters.title: Reading mail: POP3, IMAP, JMAP and Sieve
chapters.part: How email works
chapters.summary: How mail apps get mail out of the server, why there are three protocols for it, and how Sieve rules sort mail before anyone reads it.
chapters.intro:
SMTP only delivers. It puts a message into Bob's mailbox and stops. Getting it out again, onto Bob's laptop and phone, is a different job, done by different protocols, usually by a different program on the server: Dovecot or Cyrus next to Postfix, for example.

Three protocols do that job, from three eras: POP3 from when mail was read on one computer, IMAP from when people wanted it everywhere, and JMAP from when "everywhere" came to mean phones on mobile networks. A fourth standard, Sieve, runs before any of them, and decides which folder a message goes into.

The diagram's source is reading.workflow.json.

sections.title: POP3: download it
sections.html:
POP3 (RFC 1939, 1996) is the simplest. The app signs in, lists the messages, downloads them, and usually deletes them from the server. There are no folders on the server, no read flags, and no sync: a message read on the laptop is still unread on the phone, or already gone from it.

POP3 is still useful for one thing: moving mail off a server into a single archive. It is on port 110 with STLS, or 995 with TLS from the first byte.

sections.title: IMAP: keep it on the server
sections.titleHtml: IMAP: keep it on the server
sections.html:
IMAP keeps the mail on the server and lets every app see the same thing: folders, read and flagged status, and new mail as it arrives. Its current version is IMAP4rev2 (RFC 9051, 2021); almost every app and server also speaks the older IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501, 2003). It is on port 143 with STARTTLS, or 993 with TLS from the first byte.

IMAP is a conversation of tagged commands, which lets an app send several at once and match the answers:

C: a1 LOGIN bob@example.org app-password
S: a1 OK Logged in
C: a2 SELECT INBOX
S: * 3 EXISTS
S: a2 OK [READ-WRITE] Selected
C: a3 FETCH 3 (FLAGS BODY.PEEK[HEADER.FIELDS (FROM SUBJECT)])
S: * 3 FETCH (FLAGS () BODY[HEADER.FIELDS (FROM SUBJECT)] {52}
S: From: Alice <alice@example.com>
S: Subject: Lunch?
S:
S: )
S: a3 OK Fetch completed

Much of what makes IMAP pleasant comes from extensions, each its own RFC. A few worth knowing:

Extension What it does Standard
IDLE The server tells the app about new mail as it arrives, instead of the app asking every few minutes RFC 2177
UIDPLUS Tells the app the ID a message gets when it is saved or copied RFC 4315
MOVE Moves a message in one step, instead of copy, flag and delete RFC 6851
SPECIAL-USE Says which folder is Sent, Drafts, Trash or Junk, so apps do not have to guess by name RFC 6154
CONDSTORE, QRESYNC Fast resync: "what changed since I last looked?" RFC 7162
QUOTA How much space the mailbox has left RFC 9208
UTF8=ACCEPT Folder names and headers in UTF-8 RFC 6855

IMAP's weak points show on phones. IDLE needs a connection held open for each folder being watched, which a phone's operating system will not keep alive in the background, and resyncing a big mailbox over a slow network takes many round trips. That is why phone mail apps from the large providers use their own protocols, and why JMAP was written.

sections.title: JMAP: mail over HTTP
sections.html:
JMAP, the JSON Meta Application Protocol (RFC 8620, and for mail RFC 8621, 2019), does IMAP's job with JSON over HTTPS:

  • Batched requests: many operations in one request, with one round trip.
  • Changes since a state: the server gives each object type a state string; the app asks "what changed since state X?", and gets only that.
  • Push over a single connection for every folder, by EventSource or WebSocket (RFC 8887), or through a phone's own push service.
  • Sending is part of it, so an app needs one protocol and one sign-in, not IMAP plus SMTP.

Servers that implement JMAP include Fastmail, Cyrus IMAP, Stalwart and Apache James (jmap.io). Most desktop mail apps do not speak it yet, so for now it sits alongside IMAP rather than replacing it. Efforts to modernise email looks at where it stands.

sections.title: Sieve: rules that run on the server
sections.titleHtml: Sieve: rules that run on the server
sections.html:
Rules in a mail app ("move newsletters to the Reading folder") only run while the app is open, on that one device. Sieve (RFC 5228) is a small language for rules that run on the server, as mail is delivered, so the result is the same on every device:

require ["fileinto", "vacation"];

if header :contains "List-Id" "<announce.example.org>" {
  fileinto "Lists/Announce";
  stop;
}

vacation :days 7 :subject "Away until Monday"
  "I am away, and will reply when I am back.";

Sieve is deliberately limited: no loops, no variables unless an extension adds them, no access to anything but the message. That makes it safe to let every user write their own. Extensions add the rest: vacation (RFC 5230), variables (RFC 5229), imap4flags (RFC 5232) and others.

ManageSieve (RFC 5804) is the protocol mail apps use to upload and edit a user's Sieve scripts, usually on port 4190.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• POP3 on more than one device: the first device to connect takes the mail.
  • Folder names guessed: without SPECIAL-USE, one app saves sent mail in "Sent", another in "Sent Items", and the user sees two folders.
  • Passwords in the clear on 143 or 110 without STARTTLS, or a downgrade of it (Encryption in transit).
  • Rules in the app instead of on the server, so the phone sees an unsorted inbox.
  • Auto-replies that answer mailing lists and bounces, from a vacation rule that ignores RFC 3834 (Bounces, queues and retries).

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• IMAP on port 993 only, encrypted from the first byte, with IDLE, MOVE, QUOTA, UIDPLUS, UNSELECT, ENABLE, UTF8=ACCEPT and SPECIAL-USE, and with these parts of IMAP4rev2: SASL-IR, LITERAL-, NAMESPACE, ESEARCH, SEARCHRES, LIST-EXTENDED, LIST-STATUS, STATUS=SIZE and BINARY. The protocol is rest-mail/go-imap, a server library with a test for each RFC; REST Mail's gateway only supplies the mailboxes, from the REST API (internal/gateway/imap/). Sent, Drafts, Trash, Spam and Archive carry their roles (\Sent, \Drafts, \Trash, \Junk, \Archive) in LIST. It speaks IMAP4rev1; the rest of IMAP4rev2 is #718.
  • POP3 on port 995 only, from rest-mail/go-pop3 (internal/gateway/pop3/).
  • Apps that do not ask for UTF-8 get headers rewritten into ASCII, as RFC 6855 and RFC 6856 describe (internal/gateway/rawmsg/downgrade.go).
  • REST Mail's own apps use the REST API, over HTTPS, the same niche JMAP fills: batched JSON, sending and reading through one API, live updates by server-sent events for the webmail (internal/api/handlers/events.go), and push notifications to the iPhone app (internal/push/). It is not JMAP: a JMAP app cannot use it. Supporting JMAP is being designed in #720.
  • Sieve runs as a step of each domain's inbound pipeline, with rest-mail/go-sieve (internal/pipeline/filters/sieve.go). Scripts are edited through the REST API (GET and PUT /api/v1/accounts/{id}/sieve, sieve.go). ManageSieve, so mail apps can edit them too, is #719.
  • Signing in from a mail app uses an app password, because an account with two-factor authentication cannot sign in to IMAP or POP3 with its own password (Who may send).

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• POP3: RFC 1939.
  • IMAP: RFC 9051 (IMAP4rev2), RFC 3501 (IMAP4rev1), and the extensions RFC 2177, RFC 4315, RFC 6851, RFC 6154, RFC 7162, RFC 9208, RFC 6855.
  • JMAP: RFC 8620, RFC 8621, RFC 8887, jmap.io: software.
  • Sieve: RFC 5228, RFC 5229, RFC 5230, RFC 5232, ManageSieve RFC 5804.
  • REST Mail: internal/gateway/imap/, internal/gateway/pop3/, internal/pipeline/filters/sieve.go.

chapters.title: Finding the server: autoconfig, Autodiscover and SRV
chapters.part: How email works
chapters.summary: How a mail app turns an email address into server names, ports and security settings, and why a wrong answer here can send passwords in the clear.
chapters.intro:
A new mail app asks for an address and a password, and a few seconds later the mail appears. In between, it has worked out which servers to use for reading and sending, which ports, whether to encrypt from the first byte or upgrade with STARTTLS, and what username to sign in with. Nothing in an email address says any of that.

There is no single standard for it. Mail apps try several methods in turn, and use the first good answer. Each method is a small protocol of its own.

The diagram's source is discovery.workflow.json.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.html: Whatever the app finds is what it saves, and keeps using for years. A good answer means encrypted connections to the right servers. A bad one means support calls, or worse: an answer that says "port 143, no encryption" makes the app send the user's password in the clear. That is why the methods below are tried in order of how much they can be trusted, and why RFC 8314 tells apps to ignore any advertised setting that does not use TLS.

sections.title: Autoconfig: ask the provider
sections.html:
Autoconfig began in Thunderbird, and is now being standardised at the IETF as draft-ietf-mailmaint-autoconfig (an Internet-Draft, last revised in June 2026; not yet an RFC). The app asks the mail provider for an XML file describing its servers, at these addresses, in order (§4.1):

  1. https://autoconfig.example.org/mail/config-v1.1.xml?emailaddress=bob@example.org
  2. https://example.org/.well-known/autoconfig/mail/config-v1.1.xml
  3. http://autoconfig.example.org/mail/config-v1.1.xml (plain HTTP, for older setups)

The answer looks like this:

<clientConfig version="1.1">
  <emailProvider id="example.org">
    <domain>example.org</domain>
    <incomingServer type="imap">
      <hostname>mail.example.org</hostname>
      <port>993</port>
      <socketType>SSL</socketType>
      <username>%EMAILADDRESS%</username>
      <authentication>password-cleartext</authentication>
    </incomingServer>
    <outgoingServer type="smtp">
      <hostname>mail.example.org</hostname>
      <port>465</port>
      <socketType>SSL</socketType>
      <username>%EMAILADDRESS%</username>
      <authentication>password-cleartext</authentication>
    </outgoingServer>
  </emailProvider>
</clientConfig>

socketType SSL means TLS from the first byte; STARTTLS means connect in the clear and upgrade. password-cleartext means the password is sent as it is, which is safe only inside that TLS connection.

If the provider has no file, the app tries the ISPDB, a central database of settings for large providers. The draft says it covers "most mail providers with a market share larger than 0.1%" (§4.2). Then it looks up the domain's MX record, and asks the company that runs the MX, because many domains' mail is hosted by someone else (§4.3).

The draft also says what a server should not do: reveal which addresses exist. "Autoconfig servers SHOULD return a real configuration, even if the email address sent as URL parameter does not exist" (§4.1.1).

sections.title: Autodiscover: Microsoft's way
sections.html: Outlook and Exchange use Autodiscover. Outlook sends an XML request to https://example.org/autodiscover/autodiscover.xml or https://autodiscover.example.org/autodiscover/autodiscover.xml, and gets the settings back in Microsoft's format (Microsoft: Autodiscover service). It was built for Exchange, and for Microsoft 365 it also finds Exchange's own protocols, but it can describe IMAP and SMTP servers too.

sections.title: SRV records: ask the DNS
sections.html:
RFC 6186 puts the same information in the DNS, as SRV records:

_submissions._tcp.example.org.  SRV  0 1 465 mail.example.org.
_imaps._tcp.example.org.        SRV  0 1 993 mail.example.org.
_pop3s._tcp.example.org.        SRV  0 1 995 mail.example.org.
_submission._tcp.example.org.   SRV  0 0 0   .
_imap._tcp.example.org.         SRV  0 0 0   .
_pop3._tcp.example.org.         SRV  0 0 0   .

A target of . means "not offered here": with those last three lines, an app knows not to try the unencrypted ports at all (RFC 6186 §3.4). _submissions (with an s), for submission on 465, was added by RFC 8314 §5.1.

SRV records have a weakness: without DNSSEC, an attacker who can answer DNS queries can point an app anywhere. RFC 6186 says an app must check the server's certificate against the domain, not just against the host name the SRV record gave (§6).

sections.title: Apple: profiles
sections.html: Apple's Mail can be set up from a configuration profile: a .mobileconfig file, which a provider offers for download, holding the account's servers and settings (Apple: Mail payload settings).

sections.title: Guessing, and asking
sections.html: When nothing works, many apps guess common names (imap.example.org, mail.example.org) and try them. The autoconfig draft asks apps to rank guessing below the secure methods, and to show the user the domain names they found before saving them, so a lookalike domain is noticed (§4.5, §5.1). Last of all, the user types the settings in by hand.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• No autoconfig, no SRV records: every app guesses, and some guess STARTTLS on 143 or 587, or no encryption at all.
  • An autoconfig file that advertises cleartext or STARTTLS when the server offers implicit TLS.
  • SRV records for ports nobody listens on, or missing . records for the services that are not offered.
  • A certificate that does not cover autoconfig. or autodiscover., so the lookup fails over HTTPS and the app falls back to weaker methods.
  • Usernames that are not the email address, which autoconfig can only express awkwardly; the draft asks servers to accept the address as the login name (§4.1.1).

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Autoconfig is served at both HTTPS addresses, and Autodiscover at /autodiscover/autodiscover.xml. Both describe IMAP on 993 and SMTP on 465, TLS from the first byte, with the email address as the login name. They never advertise a cleartext or STARTTLS port, because REST Mail does not listen on one (internal/api/handlers/autoconfig.go).
  • The server they name is the mail host, GATEWAY_HOSTNAME, the name the MX record points to and the certificate covers, never the email domain itself, which is usually a website (#722).
  • The address is optional, as the draft has it: without ?emailaddress=, the domain is the host the request was made to, autoconfig.<domain> or, at the .well-known address, the domain itself (#721).
  • SRV records are in the set REST Mail prints for a domain (chore dns:show) and checks (chore dns:check): the six records above, the implicit-TLS services on the mail host and "." for the cleartext ones, with ports read from the listeners' own settings (internal/dns/mail_records.go, #712).
  • Apple profiles are not offered.

sections.html:

  • Microsoft: Autodiscover service in Exchange Server.
  • SRV: RFC 6186, RFC 8314 §5.1, RFC 2782.
  • Apple: Mail payload settings.

chapters.title: Encryption in transit: STARTTLS and implicit TLS
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: How mail is encrypted between servers and apps, why the way it was added leaves it open to downgrade, and what to do about it.
chapters.intro:
SMTP was designed in 1982 to send everything in plain text, across networks run by people who trusted each other. Anyone on the path between two mail servers could read every message, and change it.

Encryption was added in 1999, as an upgrade a server could offer and a client could take: STARTTLS (RFC 2487, now RFC 3207). It worked: today almost all mail between large providers is encrypted. Google reports that 98 to 99% of the mail Gmail sent to other providers between July and October 2026 was encrypted in transit (Google Transparency Report). But the way it was added, as an optional upgrade offered in the clear, leaves a gap that an attacker on the path can use.

The diagram's source is starttls.sequence.json.

sections.title: Two ways to encrypt
sections.html:
• STARTTLS: connect in the clear, ask "do you support encryption?", and upgrade the same connection if the answer is yes.
  • Implicit TLS: connect to a port where TLS starts with the first byte, the way HTTPS does. There is no unencrypted moment.
Port Used for Encryption
25 Server to server STARTTLS, optional
587 Submission, from mail apps STARTTLS
465 Submission, from mail apps Implicit TLS
143 / 993 IMAP STARTTLS / implicit TLS
110 / 995 POP3 STARTTLS (STLS) / implicit TLS

For connections from mail apps, the IETF now prefers implicit TLS. RFC 8314, "Cleartext Considered Obsolete" (2018), asks providers to offer submission on 465, IMAP on 993 and POP3 on 995, and apps to use them.

sections.title: Why port 25 cannot require encryption
sections.html:
Between servers, there is only one port, 25, and it has to start in the clear, because the sender cannot know in advance whether the receiver supports encryption. And a server that receives mail for a domain must not refuse it for being unencrypted: "A publicly-referenced SMTP server MUST NOT require use of the STARTTLS extension in order to deliver mail locally" (RFC 3207 §4).

So encryption between servers is opportunistic: used when both sides can, skipped when they cannot. RFC 7435 describes the idea: "The primary goal of OS is to not impede communication while maximizing the deployment of usable security."

sections.title: The downgrade
sections.html:
The offer to encrypt travels in the clear, in the EHLO reply. Anyone who can change traffic on the path can delete the line 250-STARTTLS. The sending server then sees a receiver that does not support encryption, and, being opportunistic, sends the message in plain text. Neither side notices.

This is not hypothetical. In 2014 the EFF reported "ISPs in the US and Thailand intercepting their customers' data to strip a security flag—called STARTTLS—from email traffic", and firewalls that did the same (EFF, 2014).

sections.title: Certificates nobody checks
sections.html:
Even when the upgrade happens, the sending server usually does not check who it is talking to. A certificate proves the server's name, but on port 25 there is no standard way to know which name to expect, or whether to insist. So most servers accept any certificate, and most receivers' certificates would fail a check: a 2023 study of the top 10 million domains found that over 96% of reachable MX servers offer STARTTLS, but "30% of presented certificates are invalid, mostly because of hostname issues", and every one of the 47 mail providers it tested delivered to servers with expired, self-signed or mismatched certificates (Blechschmidt and Stock, USENIX Security 2023).

That is encryption against someone listening, not against someone who can redirect the connection to their own server. Closing that gap, by publishing which names and certificates to expect, is what MTA-STS and DANE are for.

sections.title: STARTTLS is hard to implement
sections.html: Upgrading a connection halfway through is subtle. In 2011, Postfix's author found that many servers, Postfix included, would treat commands an attacker injected in the clear, right after STARTTLS, as if they had arrived encrypted (Postfix: CVE-2011-0411). In 2021, a study of 28 mail apps and 23 servers found more than 40 STARTTLS flaws, some of which let an attacker steal passwords or show a user forged mailbox contents, and recommended implicit TLS wherever possible (Poddebniak et al., USENIX Security 2021, nostarttls.secvuln.info).

sections.title: Asking for encryption, per message
sections.html:
Two newer standards let a sender say what it needs:

  • REQUIRETLS (RFC 8689): this message may only travel over TLS to an authenticated server, on every hop, or it must bounce.
  • TLS-Required: No (the same RFC): ignore the recipient's TLS policy for this one message, for example to tell them their certificate has expired.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• Requiring TLS on port 25. Mail from senders that cannot encrypt bounces.
  • Offering sign-in before encryption, on 587 or 143 without STARTTLS, so a password can cross the network in the clear.
  • Expired or mismatched certificates. Most senders still deliver, but MTA-STS and DANE senders will not, and mail apps show warnings users learn to click through.
  • Old TLS versions. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996, 2021).
  • Trusting STARTTLS alone for anything that matters, when it can be stripped.

sections.title: Check your own server
sections.html:
# Port 25: is STARTTLS offered, and what certificate comes back?
openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect mx.example.org:25 -servername mx.example.org -brief

# Submission and IMAP over implicit TLS
openssl s_client -connect mail.example.org:465 -brief
openssl s_client -connect mail.example.org:993 -brief

Look at the protocol version, and whether the certificate's name matches the host name the MX record gives.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Port 25 offers STARTTLS on every connection, and accepts mail without it, as RFC 3207 requires. A message that arrives unencrypted is recorded as such, so filters can treat it with more suspicion (internal/gateway/smtp/session.go, Mail; #292).
  • Every other port is implicit TLS only: submission on 465, IMAP on 993, POP3 on 995, as RFC 8314 prefers. There is no setting for 587, 143 or 110, and a production server refuses to start without a certificate (internal/config/config.go).
  • TLS 1.2 or later on every listener.
  • Certificates are chosen by the name the client asked for (SNI), reloaded without a restart when they are renewed, and renewed with ACME (internal/gateway/tlsutil/, internal/acme/).
  • STARTTLS command injection: after the handshake, REST Mail's SMTP library reads from a fresh reader on the encrypted connection, so nothing sent in the clear alongside STARTTLS is read as if it had been encrypted (rest-mail/go-smtp).
  • Sending: REST Mail uses STARTTLS whenever the receiver offers it, and enforces a recipient's MTA-STS policy. With no policy it is opportunistic, as RFC 7435 and Postfix are: it encrypts whatever the certificate, checks it, and records each delivery as authenticated, encrypted or cleartext (restmail_outbound_transport_total), never calling an unverified certificate authenticated. A handshake that fails is retried on a new connection without TLS (internal/gateway/queue/worker.go, #723).
  • TLS-Required: No is honoured: a message that carries it goes without the recipient's MTA-STS policy, its policy not even looked up, with STARTTLS still used whenever the MX offers it (RFC 8689 §4.2.2). REQUIRETLS itself is not supported yet: #724.

sections.html:

chapters.title: MTA-STS, TLS-RPT, DANE and DNSSEC
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: How a domain tells senders "always use TLS, and only with these servers", the two standards that do it, and the reports that say when it fails.
chapters.intro:
Encryption in transit ended with two gaps in opportunistic STARTTLS: an attacker can delete the offer to encrypt, and the sender does not check the certificate, so an attacker who redirects the connection can answer with their own. Both gaps have the same cause. The sender has no trustworthy way to know, before it connects, that this domain always uses TLS, and which servers are really its MX.

Two standards give it that knowledge, in different ways:

  • MTA-STS publishes a policy over HTTPS, protected by the same certificate authorities as the web.
  • DANE publishes the servers' keys in the DNS, protected by DNSSEC.

A third, TLS-RPT, sends the domain a daily report of what went wrong, so it finds out before its mail does.

The diagram's source is mta-sts.workflow.json.

sections.title: MTA-STS: a policy over HTTPS
sections.html:
MTA-STS (RFC 8461, 2018) needs two things from the receiving domain. A TXT record says a policy exists, and gives its version:

_mta-sts.example.org.  TXT  "v=STSv1; id=20261023T120000"

And a web server at mta-sts.example.org serves the policy at a fixed address, https://mta-sts.example.org/.well-known/mta-sts.txt:

version: STSv1
mode: enforce
mx: mx1.example.org
mx: *.backup.example.org
max_age: 604800
  • mode is enforce (refuse to deliver without valid TLS), testing (deliver anyway, but report failures), or none (withdraw the policy).
  • mx lists the only names allowed to receive mail for the domain. An MX record pointing anywhere else is ignored.
  • max_age is how long, in seconds, a sender keeps the policy: here, a week. RFC 8461 allows up to a year.

A sender that knows the policy delivers only to a listed MX, over TLS, with a certificate valid for that MX's name. If it cannot, it keeps the message and retries, rather than sending it in the clear.

The policy is fetched over HTTPS, so an attacker would need a valid certificate for mta-sts.example.org to fake it. The weakness is the first contact: a sender that has never seen the policy can be fooled by an attacker who blocks the TXT lookup. After that, the cached policy protects every delivery until it expires, which is why senders "SHOULD proactively refresh cached policies before they expire" (§3.3).

The id is how senders notice a change: "To see if an updated policy is available [...], the sender need only check the TXT record's version "id" against the cached value" (§3). Change the policy without changing the id, and senders keep the old one.

Gmail was the first large provider to apply MTA-STS policies, in 2019 (Google Security Blog, 2019).

sections.title: DANE: keys in signed DNS
sections.html:
DANE for SMTP (RFC 7672, 2015) takes a different route. The domain signs its DNS with DNSSEC (RFC 4033), so that answers can be checked, and publishes a TLSA record for each MX (RFC 6698):

_25._tcp.mx1.example.org.  TLSA  3 1 1  2bb1...e9f0

3 1 1 means: the server's own key (3), its public key rather than the whole certificate (1), hashed with SHA-256 (1). A sender that finds a signed TLSA record must use TLS, and must check the server's key against it. The offer to encrypt can no longer be stripped, and no certificate authority is involved.

DANE is stronger than MTA-STS, with no first-contact gap, but it needs DNSSEC on both sides: on the receiving domain's zone, and in the sending server's resolver. When both apply, DANE wins: senders "MUST NOT allow MTA-STS Policy validation to override a failing DANE validation" (RFC 8461 §2). Microsoft's Exchange Online has accepted mail with inbound DANE since October 2024 (BleepingComputer, 2024).

The hard part is key rotation. A TLSA record that names a key must change before the key does: "Two TLSA records MUST be published before employing a new EE or TA public key or certificate" (RFC 7672 §4). A server whose certificate is renewed with a new key every 60 days, and whose TLSA record is not updated first, stops receiving mail from DANE senders.

sections.title: TLS-RPT: being told what went wrong
sections.titleHtml: TLS-RPT: being told what went wrong
sections.html:
TLS-RPT (RFC 8460) gives a domain a place to receive reports:

_smtp._tls.example.org.  TXT  "v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tls-reports@example.org"

Sending servers that support it send one JSON report a day, listing how many sessions succeeded and why others failed: no STARTTLS, a certificate that did not match, an expired certificate, a policy that could not be fetched. Without it, a broken MTA-STS policy shows up only as mail that never arrives.

sections.title: Mixed adoption
sections.html: A 2023 study of email security found that "MTA-STS is gaining traction slowly", supported by six of the 47 providers it tested, and that DANE records were looked up but "neither is validated or enforced by all providers" (Blechschmidt and Stock, USENIX Security 2023). The protections only work between senders and receivers that both take part.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• mode: enforce with an MX not in the mx list, after adding a new mail server. Senders that cached the policy stop delivering.
  • A certificate on mta-sts. that expires, so the policy cannot be fetched or refreshed.
  • Changing the policy without changing the id, so senders keep the old one until max_age runs out.
  • A new key without a new TLSA record first, cutting off DANE senders.
  • DNSSEC that breaks: an expired signature makes the whole zone fail to resolve for validating resolvers, mail included.
  • No TLS-RPT, so none of the above is noticed.

Start with mode: testing and TLS-RPT, read the reports for a few weeks, then switch to enforce.

sections.title: Check your own domain
sections.html:
dig +short TXT _mta-sts.example.org
curl -s https://mta-sts.example.org/.well-known/mta-sts.txt
dig +short TXT _smtp._tls.example.org
dig +dnssec +short TLSA _25._tcp.mx1.example.org

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Sending: REST Mail fetches each recipient domain's MTA-STS policy before choosing how to deliver, and an enforce policy is applied to every path, SMTP and RESTMAIL alike: no listed MX with valid TLS, no delivery (internal/gateway/queue/worker.go, rest-mail/go-mtasts; MTASTS_ENFORCE, on by default).
  • Receiving: an administrator sets a domain's policy through the admin API, and REST Mail serves it at /.well-known/mta-sts.txt for mta-sts.<domain>, internationalised domains included (internal/api/handlers/mtasts.go). chore dns:show prints the domain's _mta-sts record, v=STSv1; id=<id>, with an id derived from the policy file itself (a SHA-256 of what senders fetch), so it changes exactly when the policy does and the operator never picks one; chore dns:check reports a published id the policy has moved on from (internal/db/models/mtasts.go). The mta-sts.<domain> host record, and a certificate covering that name, are not printed or obtained yet: #727.
  • TLS-RPT: REST Mail accepts reports sent to it over HTTPS, at /.well-known/smtp-tlsrpt, with limits on size and rate (tlsrpt.go), and chore dns:show prints each domain's _smtp._tls record pointing there, on the mail host. It sends them too: the queue counts what each outbound SMTP session's TLS came to, and once a day every recipient domain that publishes an _smtp._tls record gets the day before's report, by HTTPS or by mail signed with the DKIM key of REST Mail's own domain (tlsrpt_report.go). An MTA-STS policy it could not fetch, authenticate or read is reported as that failure. It also accepts reports by email at an existing mailbox configured with TLSRPT_REPORT_ADDRESS (api.tlsReportAddress in the chart). Publish a mailto: URI for that mailbox in the domain's _smtp._tls record to use it. Reports must be multipart/report; report-type=tlsrpt, contain a JSON or gzip report, and carry a valid full-body DKIM signature from the reporting domain (RFC 8460 §§3 and 5.3). Recognised reports are consumed into the same table as HTTPS reports; unsigned or invalid reports are ignored. Ordinary mail still reaches the mailbox. Both the compressed and inflated report are capped at 512 KiB, the email at 1 MiB, and the report at 100 policy entries. Email ingestion is disabled when the address is empty. DNS output continues to advertise the HTTPS endpoint.
  • DANE publication preparation: restmail tlsa-records computes 3 1 1 records from the SMTP public certificate, with an optional staged key for rollover. chore dns:show --tlsa-cert current.pem --tlsa-next-cert staged.pem includes those candidates. See preparing TLSA records for the DNSSEC prerequisites and rollover sequence. Automatic safe certificate/key renewal remains in #725; the current ACME renewal rotates keys and must be coordinated before publishing TLSA.
  • DANE when sending: with DANE_RESOLVER set to a DNSSEC-validating resolver on the same host (a loopback address), the queue applies DANE for SMTP (RFC 7672) to recipient domains whose MX records are DNSSEC-secure. An MX host with usable TLSA records gets the message only over TLS its records authenticate, and those records, not MTA-STS, decide that host's TLS. A bogus answer, a resolver that does not answer, a missing STARTTLS or a certificate no record matches defers the message; it is never sent to that host in the clear. Unset, DANE is off (internal/dane, dane.go). DANE sessions are in the recipient domain's TLS-RPT report under policy type tlsa, with the host's TLSA records as the policy strings: a certificate no record matches is tlsa-invalid, TLSA records that fail DNSSEC validation dnssec-invalid.
