chapters.title: Who may send: SMTP AUTH, SASL and app passwords
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: Why a mail server needs two front doors, how sign-in works over SMTP, and what limits keep one stolen password from becoming a spam machine.
chapters.intro:
A mail server takes mail from two kinds of client, and must treat them completely differently:

  • Other servers, delivering mail to your users. Anyone in the world may do this, without signing in, but only for addresses you host.
  • Your own users, sending mail anywhere in the world. Only they may do this, and the server has to know who they are.

Mixing the two up is how a server becomes an open relay. Keeping them apart is the job of separate ports, a sign-in, and limits on what a signed-in user may do.

The diagram's source is who-may-send.workflow.json.

sections.title: Two doors
sections.html:
Until the late 1990s, mail apps sent mail the same way servers did, on port 25, and servers decided who to relay for by IP address. As people started sending from home connections, hotels and phones, addresses stopped meaning anything. The fix was to give users their own door: message submission (RFC 6409, first published as RFC 2476 in 1998), on port 587, or 465 with TLS from the first byte (RFC 8314).

On the submission door, signing in is required: "The MSA MUST, by default, issue an error response to the MAIL command if the session has not been authenticated" (RFC 6409 §4.3). On port 25, the server is an MX: it accepts mail only for its own domains, and need not offer sign-in at all.

sections.title: How signing in works: SMTP AUTH and SASL
sections.titleHtml: How signing in works: SMTP AUTH and SASL
sections.html:
SMTP's sign-in is the AUTH command (RFC 4954). It does not define how to prove who you are; it borrows that from SASL, the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (RFC 4422), which IMAP and POP3 use too. The server lists the methods it accepts, and the client picks one:

S: 250-AUTH PLAIN LOGIN
C: AUTH PLAIN AGJvYkBleGFtcGxlLm9yZwBzZWNyZXQ=
S: 235 2.7.0 Authentication successful
Mechanism How it works Notes
PLAIN Sends the username and password, base64-encoded (not encrypted) Safe only inside TLS (RFC 4616)
LOGIN The same, in two steps Never standardised, but almost every app supports it
SCRAM-SHA-256 Proves knowledge of the password without sending it RFC 7677; fewer apps support it
OAUTHBEARER, XOAUTH2 Sends a token from a separate sign-in, often in a browser RFC 7628; used by Gmail and Microsoft 365

PLAIN is the most common, and its own standard warns that it "should not be used without adequate data security protection as this mechanism affords no integrity or confidentiality protections itself" (RFC 4616 §1). Over implicit TLS on 465, that protection is there from the first byte.

sections.title: Passwords leak, so use app passwords
sections.titleHtml: Passwords leak, so use app passwords
sections.html:
A mail app stores the password and sends it on every connection, for years. If it is the same password the user signs in to everything else with, one leak gives a spammer the account, and with it the right to send anywhere. Spamhaus has called stolen SMTP passwords "a major vector for criminal spam" (Spamhaus, 2012), and in 2024 still keeps a dedicated blocklist for it (Spamhaus, 2024).

Mail protocols also cannot ask for a second factor: there is no place in AUTH PLAIN for a code from an authenticator app. The common answer is the app password: a long, random password, made for one app or device, which can be revoked without changing anything else. The large providers have moved away from ordinary passwords for mail apps entirely:

  • Google turned off sign-in with an account's ordinary password for IMAP, POP and SMTP apps on March 14, 2025; such apps now need OAuth or an app password (Google Workspace Admin Help).
  • Microsoft turned off Basic authentication for POP, IMAP and most other protocols in Exchange Online from October 1, 2022, and disabled SMTP AUTH in tenants that were not using it (Microsoft Learn).

sections.title: After sign-in: what a user may do
sections.titleHtml: After sign-in: what a user may do
sections.html:
Signing in answers "who are you?", not "what may you do?". A server still needs to check:

  • That the sender address is theirs. A signed-in user who may put any address in MAIL FROM and From: can impersonate everyone else on the server, and anyone else at all. Spamhaus recommends "disallowing sending from domains whose mail you do not host".
  • That they are within their limits: messages per hour, recipients per message. Spamhaus recommends "default per-account limits on numbers of outgoing emails" (both from Spamhaus, 2024). A stolen password is then a nuisance, not a disaster.
  • That nobody is guessing. Bots try common passwords on every submission and IMAP server they find. Locking out an address after a few failures, with tools such as fail2ban, keeps that slow.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• AUTH offered on port 25. Servers never sign in to each other, so the only ones using it there are password-guessing bots.
  • AUTH before TLS, on 587 or 143 without STARTTLS, so passwords cross the network readable.
  • One password for everything: the account, the mail app, the printer and the website's contact form.
  • No per-account limits, so a single stolen login sends millions of messages (The open relay and the spam machine).
  • Trusting an application by its address (mynetworks) instead of giving it its own login.
  • Letting a user send as anyone, because the sender address is never checked.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Two doors, enforced. Port 25 never offers AUTH (503 5.5.1 AUTH not available on this port), and accepts mail only for mailboxes it hosts. Port 465 is implicit TLS, offers AUTH PLAIN and AUTH LOGIN, and refuses MAIL FROM before sign-in with 530 (internal/gateway/smtp/session.go).
  • One sign-in path for every protocol. SMTP, IMAP and POP3 all check a password through the same API call, POST /api/v1/auth/protocol-sign-in, so the rules are the same everywhere.
  • App passwords: named, revocable, for mail apps and automations, usable over IMAP, POP3, SMTP and the REST API. An account with two-factor authentication can only sign in to mail apps with one; its own password is refused (internal/auth/app_password.go).
  • Only your own addresses. A signed-in account may send only from addresses it owns, or ones it holds a mail:send grant on; anything else is refused with 550. An app password sends only as its own address.
  • Limits per account, on by default: 20 messages a minute and 100 an hour on submission, and at most 100 recipients per message (internal/ratelimit/submission.go).
  • Guessing is slowed: after 5 failed sign-ins from one address within 10 minutes, that address is banned for 30 minutes; bans can also be made permanent, by hand or from fail2ban (internal/gateway/connlimiter/, docs/fail2ban-setup.md).
  • Not offered: SCRAM-SHA-256 and OAuth sign-in.

sections.html:

  • RFC 4954: SMTP AUTH. RFC 4422: SASL. RFC 4616: PLAIN. RFC 7677: SCRAM-SHA-256. RFC 7628: OAUTHBEARER.

chapters.title: SPF: which servers may send for a domain
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: How SPF lets a domain list the servers allowed to send its mail, how a receiver checks it, the 10-lookup limit, and why forwarding breaks it.
chapters.intro:
Nothing in SMTP stops a server from saying MAIL FROM:<ceo@example.com> when it has nothing to do with example.com. For decades, receivers had no way to tell.

SPF, the Sender Policy Framework, gives the domain a way to say which servers may send its mail. It is a single DNS record, and the receiving server checks the connecting address against it (RFC 7208, 2014, after the experimental RFC 4408 of 2006).

The diagram's source is spf.workflow.json.

sections.title: The record
sections.html:
example.com.  TXT  "v=spf1 mx ip4:203.0.113.0/24 include:_spf.mailer.example -all"

Read it left to right, as a receiver does:

  1. mx: the domain's own MX servers may send.
  2. ip4:203.0.113.0/24: so may any address in this range (ip6: for IPv6).
  3. include:_spf.mailer.example: so may any server the newsletter service lists in its own SPF record.
  4. -all: nobody else.

The first term that matches the connecting address decides. Each term can carry a qualifier saying what a match means: + pass (the default), - fail, ~ softfail ("probably not, but do not reject on this alone"), ? neutral. So -all at the end means "everything else fails", and ~all means "everything else is suspicious".

The other terms are a (the domain's own addresses), exists (a DNS name built from the sender and the connecting address, for special cases), redirect= (use another domain's record instead), and ptr, which "SHOULD NOT be published" (§5.5), because it is slow and unreliable.

sections.title: What gets checked
sections.html:
SPF checks two identities, both from the SMTP conversation, not from the message:

  • MAIL FROM, the envelope sender: the main check.
  • HELO, the name the client greeted with. RFC 7208 recommends checking it too, and first (§2.3). For a bounce, which has an empty MAIL FROM, it is the only identity.

The result is one of seven (§2.6):

Result Meaning
pass The address is allowed to send for the domain
fail The domain says it is not
softfail The domain says probably not
neutral The domain makes no statement about this address
none The domain has no SPF record
temperror A DNS problem; try again later
permerror The record is broken: a syntax error, or too many lookups

Note what SPF does not check: the From: line the reader sees. A message can pass SPF for MAIL FROM:<bounces@mailer.example> while its From: says ceo@example.com. Tying the two together is DMARC's job.

sections.title: The 10-lookup limit
sections.html:
Each include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect costs the receiver a DNS query, and an include can include others. To keep that bounded, "SPF implementations MUST limit the total number of those terms to 10 during SPF evaluation [...] If this limit is exceeded, the implementation MUST return "permerror"" (§4.6.4). Lookups that find nothing ("void lookups") should be limited to two.

This is the most common way a well-meaning domain breaks its own SPF. Every service it sends through (a newsletter tool, a helpdesk, a CRM, the office suite) asks to be included, each include brings its own lookups, and one day the eleventh pushes the record into permerror. Everything then fails SPF, the domain's own mail included.

sections.title: Why forwarding breaks SPF
sections.html:
Bob forwards his mail from bob@old.example to bob@new.example. A message from Alice arrives at old.example, and is passed on to new.example with Alice's envelope sender unchanged, as forwarding traditionally does (RFC 5321 §3.9.1). Now new.example sees a message claiming to be from example.com, arriving from old.example's server, which is not in example.com's SPF record. SPF fails, through no one's fault.

Two fixes exist:

  • SRS, the Sender Rewriting Scheme: the forwarder rewrites the envelope sender to an address of its own, so SPF is checked against the forwarder's domain, and bounces come back to the forwarder, which passes them on. SRS is not an RFC; for Postfix it is usually added with PostSRSd.
  • ARC: the forwarder records that the message passed SPF when it arrived, and signs that record, so the final receiver can choose to trust it.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• More than 10 lookups, so SPF is a permerror for everything.
  • Two SPF records on one name: that is a permerror too (§3.2).
  • +all, which allows the whole internet, or ?all, which says nothing.
  • ~all forever, published as a first step and never tightened.
  • A new mail service, not added, whose mail then fails SPF.
  • IPv6 forgotten: the server sends over IPv6 and only its IPv4 address is listed.
  • No SPF record at all. A 2023 study of the top 10 million domains found that "only about 40% of sites publish SPF" (Blechschmidt and Stock, USENIX Security 2023).

A domain that sends no mail at all should still publish v=spf1 -all, so that nobody can use it.

sections.title: Check your own domain
sections.html:
dig +short TXT example.com | grep spf1      # exactly one record
dig +short TXT _spf.mailer.example          # and each include, for its own lookups

Count every include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect, following includes into the records they name. The total must be 10 or fewer.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• The record it asks you to publish is v=spf1 mx -all: the domain's MX may send, nothing else. It names the MX rather than an address, so moving the server changes one A record and nothing else (internal/dns/mail_records.go).
  • Incoming mail is checked by the spf_check filter, for both the HELO and the MAIL FROM identity, with rest-mail/go-spf, which enforces the 10-lookup and 2-void-lookup limits (internal/pipeline/filters/spf_check.go).
  • SPF alone does not reject, by default. The result is recorded for DMARC, which decides with the From: domain's own policy. A domain can make an SPF fail reject or quarantine instead, with the filter's fail_action.
  • The result is written into the message, as an Authentication-Results field (RFC 8601), and any field that arrived claiming to be from this server is removed first, so a sender cannot forge a pass (internal/mime/authresults.go).
  • Forwarding: REST Mail's Sieve redirects keep the original envelope sender, so forwarded mail can fail SPF at the next hop. Rewriting it with SRS, and bouncing failed forwards correctly, is discussed in #715.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF), version 1. RFC 4408: the 2006 experimental version.
  • RFC 5321 §3.9: aliases and forwarding.
  • RFC 8601: Authentication-Results.
  • Blechschmidt and Stock: Extended Hell(o), USENIX Security 2023.
  • REST Mail: internal/pipeline/filters/spf_check.go, rest-mail/go-spf.

chapters.title: DKIM: signing the message itself
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: How DKIM signatures prove a message came from a domain and was not changed, how keys and selectors work, and the ordinary things that break a signature.
chapters.intro:
SPF checks the path a message took: which server handed it over. That breaks as soon as the message takes a different path, through a forwarder or a mailing list, and it says nothing about whether the message was changed on the way.

DKIM, DomainKeys Identified Mail, signs the message itself (RFC 6376, 2011, after RFC 4871 of 2007). The sending domain adds a cryptographic signature over the body and the important header lines, and publishes the key that checks it in the DNS. Any server, anywhere along the way, can then check that the message really was signed by that domain and has not been changed since.

The diagram's source is dkim.sequence.json.

sections.title: The signature
sections.html:
The sending server adds one header line, shown here unfolded:

DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed; d=example.com;
  s=2026a; t=1792760400; h=from:to:subject:date:message-id:mime-version;
  bh=2jUSOH9NhtVGCQWNr9BrIAPreKQjO6Sn7XIkfJVOzv8=;
  b=dzdVyOfAKCdLXdJOc9G2q8LoXSlEniSbav+yuU4zGeeruD00lszZVoG4ZHRNiYzR...
Tag Meaning
d= The signing domain: who takes responsibility for the message
s= The selector: which of the domain's keys was used
a= The algorithm: rsa-sha256, or ed25519-sha256 (RFC 8463)
h= The header lines that were signed, in order
bh= A hash of the body
b= The signature itself, over the signed header lines and bh=
c= How the message was normalised before hashing: simple or relaxed

The receiver fetches the public key from <selector>._domainkey.<domain>:

2026a._domainkey.example.com.  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8A..."

It hashes the body and the listed header lines the same way the sender did, and checks the signature with the key. If anything signed has changed, by a single character, the check fails.

sections.title: Normalising: simple and relaxed
sections.html:
Mail servers make harmless changes on the way: re-folding long header lines, changing the case of header names, adding or trimming spaces at line ends. The c= tag says how forgiving the check is (§3.4):

  • simple tolerates almost nothing.
  • relaxed ignores the case of header names, folding, and runs of spaces.

relaxed/relaxed (header/body) is the usual choice.

sections.title: Selectors and keys
sections.html:
The selector lets one domain have many keys at once: one per mail service it uses, one for each period of time. That is what makes rotation possible: publish a new key under a new selector, start signing with it, and remove the old one once mail signed with it has been delivered.

  • Key size. "Signers MUST use RSA keys of at least 1024 bits for all keys. Signers SHOULD use RSA keys of at least 2048 bits," and the old rsa-sha1 "MUST NOT be used for signing or verifying" (RFC 8301). Short keys are not a theoretical risk: in 2012, after it was shown that mail from companies with weak keys could be forged, M3AAWG urged senders to "replace previously secure 512- and 768-bit verification keys with 1024-bit and higher encryption" (M3AAWG, 2012).
  • Rotation. "DKIM keys should be rotated at least every six months" (M3AAWG, DKIM Key Rotation Best Common Practices, 2019), so that a stolen key is useful for months at most, and so that changing keys in an emergency is a routine everyone has practised.

sections.title: What breaks a signature
sections.html:
A valid signature can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with forgery:

  • Mailing lists that add a footer, or a [list-name] tag to the subject, change signed content. This is the most common cause, and why ARC exists.
  • Security gateways and antivirus that add "scanned by" lines or disclaimers to the body.
  • Re-encoding. A relay that converts an 8-bit body to quoted-printable for a 7-bit hop changes every byte the body hash covered.
  • Unsigned or wrongly signed headers. "The From header field MUST be signed" (§5.4), and a sender that signs header lines that relays routinely rewrite loses the signature for no benefit.
  • The key is gone. A selector removed from DNS too early, or not moved when the DNS host changed, fails every message still in transit.

Two features exist mostly to warn against. The l= tag signs only the first part of the body, so lists can append to it; RFC 6376 warns that it "enables attacks in which an intermediary with malicious intent can modify a message to include content that solely benefits the attacker" (§8.2). And a valid signature can be replayed: a spammer who gets one message signed by a reputable domain can send that exact message to millions, and every copy verifies (§8.6).

sections.title: DKIM is not about the From line, yet
sections.titleHtml: DKIM is not about the From line, yet
sections.html: The signing domain d= can be anything: a newsletter service signs with its own domain for all its customers. A message from ceo@example.com signed by d=mailer.example passes DKIM, and says nothing about whether example.com sent it. DMARC is what requires the two to match.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• No DKIM at all, or DKIM only from some of the services a domain sends through.
  • Keys shorter than 1024 bits, or still rsa-sha1.
  • A TXT record split wrongly. A 2048-bit key is longer than one DNS string (255 characters), and must be split into several strings in one record, not several records.
  • Keys never rotated, or rotated by deleting the old selector at once.
  • Body changes after signing, by the server's own footer or disclaimer feature, added after the signing step.

sections.title: Check your own domain
sections.html:
dig +short TXT 2026a._domainkey.example.com

Then send a message to an account elsewhere, open "Show original", and read the Authentication-Results line: it says dkim=pass with the domain and selector, or why not.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Every outbound message is signed, once, over its final bytes, after the Bcc line is removed and whichever way it was sent: the REST API, SMTP submission, or a message the queue relays. A domain with a key that cannot sign does not send unsigned; the message waits (internal/outbound/prepare.go, SignDKIM).
  • Keys are RSA of at least 2048 bits, as RFC 8301 recommends, or Ed25519; the library, rest-mail/go-dkim, refuses rsa-sha1 both ways (internal/outbound/dkimkey.go).
  • List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post are signed when a message carries them, which one-click unsubscribe requires (Bulk mail).
  • The DNS record each domain needs is printed by chore dns:show, and each key's age is exported as restmail_dkim_key_age_seconds (docs/dkim-key-age.md).
  • Incoming mail is checked by the dkim_verify filter, one result per signature, recorded for DMARC; by default a failing signature alone does not reject (internal/pipeline/filters/dkim.go).
  • Rotation: a per-domain interval can be saved, and the code to stage and activate a new key exists, but nothing runs it yet: #728.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures. RFC 4871: the 2007 original.
  • RFC 8301: cryptographic algorithm and key usage update. RFC 8463: Ed25519 for DKIM.
  • M3AAWG: DKIM key length best practices (2012), DKIM Key Rotation Best Common Practices (2019).
  • REST Mail: internal/outbound/, internal/pipeline/filters/dkim.go, rest-mail/go-dkim.

chapters.title: DMARC: protecting the From line
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: How DMARC ties SPF and DKIM to the address the reader sees, what p=none, quarantine and reject do, the reports, and why p=reject and mailing lists do not mix.
chapters.intro:
SPF checks the envelope sender. DKIM checks whichever domain signed. Neither checks the one address the reader actually sees: the From: line. A phishing message can pass both, with its own domain, while its From: says security@yourbank.example.

DMARC, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance, closes that gap. It says: a message whose From: is in my domain must pass SPF or DKIM for my domain, and here is what to do with one that does not. It was published in 2015 as an informational document (RFC 7489), and became an IETF standard in May 2026 as RFC 9989, with its reports in RFC 9990 and RFC 9991.

The diagram's source is dmarc.workflow.json.

sections.title: Alignment
sections.html:
DMARC's central idea is alignment: the domain that passed SPF or DKIM must be the From: domain, or belong to the same organisation.

  • SPF aligns when the MAIL FROM domain matches the From: domain.
  • DKIM aligns when a valid signature's d= matches the From: domain.

A message passes DMARC if at least one of them passes and aligns. Two strictness levels exist, set separately for each (aspf=, adkim=):

  • Relaxed (the default): the same organisation is enough. bounces.example.com aligns with example.com.
  • Strict: the names must be identical.

sections.title: The record
sections.html:
_dmarc.example.com.  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com"
Tag Meaning
p= What the domain asks receivers to do with mail that fails: none, quarantine or reject
sp= The same, for subdomains that exist
np= The same, for subdomains that do not exist (new in RFC 9989)
rua= Where to send daily aggregate reports
ruf= Where to send reports about single failing messages
adkim=, aspf= Relaxed (r) or strict (s) alignment
t=y Testing: apply one level less than the stated policy (new in RFC 9989)
psd= Whether this is a public suffix domain such as a registry (new in RFC 9989)

RFC 9989 also removed three tags: pct (apply the policy to a percentage of mail), which "was usually not accurately applied" (Appendix A.6), and rf and ri. Receivers ignore them now.

sections.title: The three policies
sections.html:
• p=none: do nothing different, but send reports. This is how every domain should start: "discovered policies of "p=none" MUST NOT modify existing mail handling processes" (RFC 9989 §5.4).
  • p=quarantine: treat failing mail as suspicious, usually the spam folder.
  • p=reject: refuse failing mail during the SMTP conversation.

The policy is a request, not a command: "The final handling of any message is always a matter of local policy and is left to the discretion of the Mail Receiver" (§5.4).

sections.title: Reports
sections.html: The rua address receives one XML report a day from each receiver that supports them: how many messages claimed your domain, from which addresses, and whether they passed SPF, DKIM and DMARC (RFC 9990). They are how a domain finds the mail it forgot about (the invoicing system, the newsletter tool) before tightening its policy, and how it sees who is forging its name.

sections.title: Why p=reject and mailing lists do not mix
sections.titleHtml: Why p=reject and mailing lists do not mix
sections.html:
A mailing list resends a member's message to every subscriber, with the member's From:. It sends from its own server, so SPF does not align; and it usually adds a footer or a [list] tag, so the DKIM signature breaks (DKIM). The message fails DMARC at every subscriber's server, through no fault of anyone.

This became visible in April 2014, when Yahoo published p=reject for yahoo.com. John Levine explained to the IETF what followed: "Lists generally modify messages via subject tags, body footers, attachment stripping, and other useful features that break the DKIM signature. So on even the most legitimate list mail like, say, the IETF's, most of the mail fails the DMARC assertions", and subscribers' servers rejected it (PCWorld, 2014). Worse, list software saw those rejections as bounces, and unsubscribed people who had done nothing wrong (RFC 7960).

The new standard draws the conclusion for both sides:

  • For domains: "domains that host users who might post messages to mailing lists SHOULD NOT publish Domain Owner Assessment Policies of "p=reject"". A domain that wants it anyway should publish p=none for at least a month, then p=quarantine for as long, and compare the reports first (RFC 9989 §7.4).
  • For receivers: they "SHOULD NOT reject messages solely because of a published policy of "reject" but [...] apply other knowledge and analysis" (§5.4).

Mailing lists adapted too, by rewriting the From: line of posts from such domains ("Alice via the List"), and ARC lets a list vouch for what a message looked like when it arrived.

sections.title: Who requires it
sections.html: Since February 2024, Gmail requires DMARC of anyone sending it more than 5,000 messages a day, though p=none is enough, and requires the From: domain to align with SPF or DKIM (Google, Email sender guidelines). Outlook.com has required the same of senders above 5,000 a day since May 5, 2025 (Microsoft, 2025). See Bulk mail.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• Jumping straight to p=reject, before the reports show every legitimate source passing, and before thinking about mailing lists.
  • Services that send as you without aligning: a newsletter tool that signs with its own d= and uses its own bounce domain passes SPF and DKIM, but not DMARC for your domain.
  • rua pointing at a mailbox nobody reads. The reports are the point of p=none.
  • Forgetting subdomains: without sp= or np=, p= applies to every subdomain, including ones invented by a forger.
  • Relying on SPF alone under p=reject: forwarding breaks SPF, so "domains that publish "p=reject" MUST NOT rely solely on SPF [...] and MUST apply valid DKIM signatures" (§7.4).

sections.title: Check your own domain
sections.html:
dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com

Then read an aggregate report, or send yourself a message at another provider and look for dmarc=pass in its Authentication-Results.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Incoming mail: the dmarc_check filter combines the SPF and DKIM results and applies the From: domain's policy: reject refuses with 550, quarantine holds the message, none changes nothing (internal/pipeline/filters/dmarc_check.go, rest-mail/go-dmarc). It follows RFC 9989: the policy and each domain's organisation come from the DNS tree walk, a subdomain that does not exist gets np, and a record in test mode (t=y) is applied one level lower. A failure that a trusted ARC sealer vouches for is let through, and a p=reject failure that came through a mailing list (it carries List-Id) is quarantined rather than refused, since a list breaks the authentication RFC 9989 relies on; each such departure from the policy is reported, with its reason. Other p=reject failures are still refused.
  • Reports: REST Mail sends RFC 9990 aggregate reports to every address a domain asks for, one report per policy domain (internal/dmarcreport/).
  • Your domain's record: chore dns:show prints a DMARC record with the domain's own policy, dmarc_policy in the admin API. A new domain starts at p=none, so its reports come in from the first day and no one's delivery changes. An admin raises it to quarantine, then reject, once the reports show the domain's mail passes, as RFC 9989 §7.4 advises, and leaves a domain whose users write to mailing lists below reject. REST Mail always signs with DKIM, which p=reject requires (#729).
  • The standard: REST Mail implements RFC 9989 and RFC 9990: no Public Suffix List, no pct. A subdomain gets np when DNS answers NXDOMAIN for it (RFC 8020); Go's resolver reports NXDOMAIN and an empty answer alike, so REST Mail asks the DNS servers itself and reads the response code (nxdomain.go). Receiving aggregate reports for REST Mail's own domains is still to come (#730).

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• RFC 9989: DMARC (May 2026). RFC 9990: aggregate reporting. RFC 9991: failure reporting. RFC 7489: the 2015 original, now obsolete.
  • RFC 7960: DMARC and indirect email flows.
  • PCWorld: Yahoo email anti-spoofing policy breaks mailing lists (2014).
  • Google: Email sender guidelines.
  • Microsoft: Outlook's new requirements for high-volume senders (2025).
  • REST Mail: internal/pipeline/filters/dmarc_check.go, internal/dmarcreport/, internal/dns/mail_records.go.

chapters.title: ARC: authentication that survives forwarding
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: How a forwarder or mailing list can record what a message's authentication looked like when it arrived, and why a receiver still has to decide whom to believe.
chapters.intro:
SPF breaks when a message is forwarded. DKIM breaks when a mailing list adds a footer. And then DMARC fails, and a domain with p=reject asks the final receiver to refuse a message that was perfectly genuine when it left.

The forwarder or list knew the message was genuine: it checked SPF, DKIM and DMARC when the message arrived. ARC, the Authenticated Received Chain, gives it a way to write that down, sign it, and pass it on (RFC 8617, 2019, published as Experimental).

The diagram's source is arc.sequence.json.

sections.title: Three header lines per hop
sections.html:
Each intermediary that takes part adds an ARC set, numbered with i=: 1 for the first, 2 for the next, and so on.

  • ARC-Authentication-Results (AAR): what this hop saw when the message arrived, in the same format as Authentication-Results, such as spf=pass dkim=pass dmarc=pass.
  • ARC-Message-Signature (AMS): a DKIM-style signature of the message as this hop sends it on, changes included.
  • ARC-Seal (AS): a signature over all the ARC sets so far, with cv=, this hop's verdict on the chain that arrived: none (there was none), pass or fail.
ARC-Seal: i=1; a=rsa-sha256; cv=none; d=lists.example.net; s=arc; b=...
ARC-Message-Signature: i=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed; d=lists.example.net; s=arc; h=from:to:subject; bh=...; b=...
ARC-Authentication-Results: i=1; lists.example.net; spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=example.com; dkim=pass header.d=example.com; dmarc=pass header.from=example.com

The final receiver checks the chain: every seal valid, every instance present, the newest message signature matching the message as it is now. If the chain holds, it knows exactly what each hop claims it saw.

sections.title: Claims, not proof
sections.html:
ARC does not prove the original message was genuine. It proves that a particular intermediary says so. A spammer can run an intermediary and seal anything. So ARC's results are only as good as the receiver's trust in the sealer, and the standard leaves that decision to the receiver: "As a matter of local policy, a DMARC processor MAY choose to accept the authentication assessments provided by an Authenticated Received Chain" (RFC 8617 §7.2.1).

In practice, receivers trust a short list of sealers they know: large providers, and the mailing list services their users depend on. Microsoft 365, for example, lets an administrator name trusted ARC sealers, whose recorded results it then uses "in email authentication checks" (Microsoft Learn).

sections.title: Where ARC fits
sections.html:
• Forwarders and mailing lists should seal, so the mail they pass on can be judged on what it was.
  • Receivers should verify, and use the results from sealers they trust when DMARC fails. When they do override a policy that way, DMARC reports have a place to say so (PolicyOverride, RFC 9990).
  • Senders need do nothing.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• Sealing without checking: an intermediary that records pass for everything makes its seals worthless.
  • Changing the message after sealing, for example a footer added by a later step, breaks the newest message signature.
  • Trusting every valid chain, which lets anyone who runs a sealer bypass DMARC.
  • Not sealing at all, so forwarded mail fails DMARC at the next hop with no evidence to rescue it.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Verifying: the arc_verify filter validates any ARC chain on incoming mail, with rest-mail/go-arc (internal/pipeline/filters/arc_verify.go).
  • Using it: when DMARC fails and the chain's latest sealer is on a domain's list of trusted sealers, the DMARC policy is overridden and the override is reported, as RFC 8617 and the DMARC reports describe. The list is empty by default (#178), so nothing is trusted until an administrator decides to.
  • Sealing: mail a Sieve redirect forwards leaves with an ARC set, sealed last, with the forwarding domain's DKIM key, over the bytes that leave. Its ARC-Authentication-Results are the SPF, DKIM, ARC and DMARC results REST Mail recorded when the message arrived, and its cv= is what arc_verify found: none for the first set, pass for a valid chain, fail for a broken one. A chain that arrived with cv=fail is passed on with no new set (RFC 8617 §5.1) (internal/outbound/arc.go, #731). A domain whose DKIM key is Ed25519 forwards unsealed, as go-arc seals with RSA alone.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• RFC 8617: The Authenticated Received Chain (ARC) Protocol.
  • RFC 9990: DMARC aggregate reporting, including policy overrides.
  • Microsoft: Configure trusted ARC sealers.
  • REST Mail: internal/pipeline/filters/arc_verify.go, internal/pipeline/filters/dmarc_check.go, rest-mail/go-arc.

chapters.title: Spam defences: blocklists, greylisting, limits and filters
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: The layers a receiving server uses to keep spam out, from cheap checks on the connection to expensive ones on the content, and what each costs legitimate senders.
chapters.intro:
Nearly half of all email is spam. Kaspersky measured that "In 2024, spam emails accounted for 47.27% of the total global email traffic" (Kaspersky, Spam and phishing in 2024). A server that accepts mail from the internet has to sort it, millions of times a day, without losing the mail that matters.

No single check does it. Defences are layered along the SMTP conversation: cheap checks first, on the connection, before the spammer has sent anything; expensive ones last, on the content. Each layer turns away what it can, and passes the rest on.

The diagram's source is spam.workflow.json.

sections.title: On the connection: who is this?
sections.titleHtml: On the connection: who is this?
sections.html:
• DNS blocklists (DNSBLs) list addresses known to send spam. The receiver reverses the connecting address and looks it up as a DNS name: for 192.0.2.99 and the list zen.example.org, it asks for 99.2.0.192.zen.example.org. An answer means listed (RFC 5782). Spamhaus and others run them; some list known spammers, others list home connections that should not send mail directly at all.
  • Reverse DNS: an address with no PTR record, or a generic one (host-192-0-2-99.dynamic.example), is very likely a home computer, not a mail server (DNS for email).
  • Talking too early: a client that sends commands before the server's greeting is almost always a bot. Postfix's postscreen waits a few seconds before greeting, to catch exactly that (POSTSCREEN_README).
  • Connection limits: too many connections from one address at once, or too many failed sign-ins, and it is slowed or banned for a while.

sections.title: In the envelope: who says they are sending, to whom?
sections.titleHtml: In the envelope: who says they are sending, to whom?
sections.html:
• SPF on the MAIL FROM and HELO identities.
  • Does the recipient exist? Refusing unknown recipients with 550 5.1.1 during the conversation, rather than bouncing later, avoids backscatter. Bots that try every common name (admin@, info@, sales@) can be slowed down after their first few misses.
  • Greylisting: refuse the first attempt from an unfamiliar combination of sending address, sender and recipient with a temporary 451, and accept the retry a few minutes later. Real mail servers retry; many spam tools did not. The idea was published by Evan Harris in 2003 (The Next Step in the Spam Control War: Greylisting), and standardised in RFC 6647 (2012). Its cost: legitimate first-time mail is delayed by minutes, sometimes more, when the sender retries from a different address.

sections.title: After the message: is it what it claims, and is it wanted?
sections.titleHtml: After the message: is it what it claims, and is it wanted?
sections.html:
• DKIM, DMARC and ARC, which need the whole message.
  • Content filters score the message on hundreds of rules: phrases, links to known bad sites, broken formatting, mismatched headers, hashes of known spam, statistical (Bayesian) models trained on each site's own mail. Common ones are Apache SpamAssassin and Rspamd. Above one score the message is junked, above a higher one refused.
  • Virus scanning, usually ClamAV.
  • Reputation: many receivers also weigh what they know of the sending domain and address over time (Deliverability).

The decision, ideally, is made before the final 250 of the conversation, so a refused message is the sender's to bounce, not yours.

sections.title: After delivery: the user
sections.html:
• The junk folder catches what scored high but not high enough to refuse.
  • "Report spam" buttons train the filters and, at large providers, feed the reputation of the sender. Senders whose mail gets reported too often are throttled or blocked (Bulk mail).

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• Blocklisting too eagerly: a blocklist that lists whole networks catches legitimate small senders on them. Know what each list you use is for.
  • Greylisting the big providers, which send from large pools of addresses and may retry from a different one each time, delaying their mail for hours.
  • Bouncing instead of refusing, and so sending backscatter.
  • Content filtering after accepting, then silently discarding: the sender thinks it was delivered, the recipient never sees it (The black hole).
  • Filters nobody watches, whose rules and training go stale.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
Each domain has an inbound pipeline of filters, run in order, each able to continue, reject, quarantine, defer or discard (internal/pipeline/, docs/adapter-filters.md):

  • Recipients are checked during the conversation: an unknown recipient is refused with 550 5.1.1, and a connection that keeps missing is slowed down, more with each miss (internal/gateway/smtp/tarpit.go).
  • Connection and sign-in limits per address, with temporary bans after repeated failed sign-ins, and fail2ban for permanent ones (internal/gateway/connlimiter/).
  • Greylisting, with the triple and its lifetime kept in the database (internal/pipeline/filters/greylist.go). REST Mail's own outbound queue retries greylisted mail after 7 minutes, so it is a good citizen on the other side too.
  • SPF, DKIM, DMARC and ARC filters (see their chapters), and rate limits per sender and domain.
  • Content and virus scanning through adapters to Rspamd and ClamAV, when they are deployed alongside (internal/pipeline/filters/rspamd.go, clamav.go).
  • Quarantine, with release and delete from the admin API, and a periodic digest to each user (internal/digest/).
  • Blocklists, for your own address: REST Mail can check its own sending addresses against DNSBLs on a schedule and report a listing (docs/dnsbl-monitor.md). Checking the addresses of servers connecting to it, an early-talker check, and reverse-DNS scoring are designed but parked (#292).

sections.html:

  • RFC 5782: DNS Blacklists and Whitelists.
  • RFC 6647: Email Greylisting: An Applicability Statement for SMTP.
  • Evan Harris: The Next Step in the Spam Control War: Greylisting (2003).

chapters.title: Bulk mail: List-Unsubscribe and the 2024 sender rules
chapters.part: The security layers, one at a time
chapters.summary: What the large mailbox providers now require of anyone sending in volume, and how one-click unsubscribe works.
chapters.intro:
Most mail is not written by a person to a person. Receipts, password resets, newsletters, notifications and marketing are sent by machines, in bulk, and much of what people call spam is mail they once agreed to and can no longer stop. In 2024 the largest mailbox providers turned years of advice into rules, and began enforcing them.

The diagram's source is unsubscribe.sequence.json.

sections.title: The rules
sections.html:
In October 2023, Google announced that "By February 2024, Gmail will start to require that bulk senders", those who send more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail addresses, authenticate their mail, offer one-click unsubscribe, and keep complaints low. Yahoo joined in: in the same announcement, its Marcel Becker said Yahoo looked forward to working with Google "to make these common sense, high-impact changes the new industry standard" (Google, 2023). Gmail's current guidelines (Email sender guidelines, FAQ):

Every sender, at any volume:

  • SPF or DKIM.
  • Valid forward and reverse DNS for sending addresses.
  • TLS for sending.
  • Messages formatted according to RFC 5322.
  • A spam rate, as reported in Postmaster Tools, below 0.3%.

Senders of 5,000 or more messages a day to Gmail, in addition:

  • SPF and DKIM.
  • A DMARC record, where p=none is enough.
  • The From: domain aligned with SPF or DKIM (DMARC).
  • One-click unsubscribe for marketing and subscribed messages, and an unsubscribe link in the body.
  • Unsubscribe requests honoured within 48 hours.

Microsoft followed for Outlook.com: from May 5, 2025, domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day must pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and mail that does not is rejected with 550 5.7.515 (Microsoft, 2025).

And the rules are being enforced: "Starting November 2025, Gmail is ramping up its enforcement on non-compliant traffic. Messages that fail to meet the email sender requirements will experience disruptions, including temporary and permanent rejections" (Google FAQ).

sections.title: List-Unsubscribe
sections.html:
The List-Unsubscribe header field has existed since 1998 (RFC 2369). It tells a mail app how to unsubscribe, so the app can offer a button next to the sender's name instead of the reader hunting for a link in small print:

List-Unsubscribe: <mailto:unsubscribe@news.example.com?subject=u-7f3a>, <https://news.example.com/u/7f3a9c2e>

A mailto: target unsubscribes by sending mail to it. An https: target used to mean "open this page", which often led to a page asking the reader to confirm, sign in, or tick boxes: one more chance to give up.

sections.title: One-click
sections.html:
RFC 8058 (2017) makes it one click. The sender adds a second header field:

List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click

and the mailbox provider, when the user presses its "Unsubscribe" button, sends an HTTPS POST with the body List-Unsubscribe=One-Click straight to the URL. No page, no confirmation. The rules that make it safe (§3.1, §4):

  • The URL identifies the recipient and the list by itself, and "SHOULD include an opaque identifier or another hard-to-forge component", so nobody can unsubscribe others by guessing.
  • The POST carries nothing else: "The POST request MUST NOT include cookies, HTTP authorization, or any other context information."
  • No redirects: "The mail sender MUST NOT return an HTTPS redirect."
  • It must be DKIM-signed: the message "MUST have a valid DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) signature that covers at least the List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post headers", so a forger cannot attach an unsubscribe URL to someone else's mail.
  • Only with the user's consent: the provider "MUST NOT perform a POST on the HTTPS URI without user consent" (§3.2), so a link-scanning filter must not trigger it.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• No List-Unsubscribe-Post, or an https target that answers the POST with a redirect or a confirmation page.
  • Unsigned unsubscribe headers, or a DKIM signature that does not cover them.
  • Unsubscribe requests honoured slowly, or not at all, so the reader presses "Report spam" instead, which raises the spam rate.
  • Transactional mail mixed with marketing on one domain and one sending address, so complaints about the newsletter hurt the delivery of password resets.
  • Spam rate above 0.3%: Gmail stops offering delivery support, and mail starts going to spam or being refused.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Unsubscribe on the send API: POST /api/v1/messages/send takes list_unsubscribe: {mailto, https}, at most one address and one HTTPS URL that the sender runs. REST Mail publishes them as List-Unsubscribe, and only an https target adds List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click. It never fetches or posts to the URL itself (internal/api/handlers/list_unsubscribe.go, #144).
  • Signed, as RFC 8058 requires: both fields are covered by the DKIM signature. A one-click target from a domain with no DKIM key is refused (422 dkim_required), because it could not be signed.
  • Checked: a target with a line break, a space, credentials, another scheme or anything that could inject a header line is refused with 400.
  • A policy per domain: a domain marked bulk must include list_unsubscribe on every send, and one marked transactional must not (422), which keeps the two kinds of mail apart. SMTP submission, draft sending and forwarding are not yet held to the policy.
  • The rest of the list above is covered elsewhere: DKIM on every message, SPF and DMARC records printed for every domain, TLS whenever the receiver offers it, and reverse DNS listed among the records to publish.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• Google: New Gmail protections for a safer, less spammy inbox (2023), Email sender guidelines, Email sender guidelines FAQ (read 2026-10-23).
  • Microsoft: Outlook's new requirements for high-volume senders (2025).
  • RFC 2369: List-Unsubscribe and the other list header fields.
  • RFC 8058: Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers.
  • REST Mail: internal/api/handlers/list_unsubscribe.go, internal/outbound/prepare.go.

chapters.title: The open relay and the spam machine
chapters.part: How it goes wrong
chapters.summary: How a mail server ends up sending strangers' spam, the four mistakes behind it, what it costs, and how to check your own.
chapters.intro:
A mail server has to do two things that pull against each other. It must accept mail from anyone on the internet, because that is how mail for your domain arrives. And it must refuse to pass mail on to anyone else, unless the sender is one of your own users. Get the first half wrong and your users miss mail. Get the second half wrong and strangers use your server to send their spam.

There are two ways to get it wrong:

  • An open relay delivers mail for anyone who connects. No password needed.
  • A spam machine delivers mail for one stolen login, as fast as it can.

Either way, the spam leaves from your server's address, and the rest of the internet holds you responsible for it.

The diagram's source is open-relay.workflow.json. On the website it is interactive: it animates, and you can follow any path through it.

sections.title: How common is it?
sections.html:
Stolen logins are a long-running, current problem. In 2012 Spamhaus wrote that spam sent "through compromised user accounts on legitimate mail servers that use SMTP AUTH authentication" had "grown precipitously" and was "a major vector for criminal spam" (Spamhaus, 2012). In 2024 it wrote that "the problem of spam through hacked accounts has been plaguing the internet for years", and it keeps a dedicated list, AuthBL, of addresses "known to host bots using brute force or stolen SMTP AUTH credentials to send spam, phishing and malware emails" (Spamhaus, 2024).

Open relays are rarer than they were, because modern servers refuse to relay by default. Each of the mistakes below brings one back. We have not found a current, reliable count of open relays on the internet. If you know of one, please open an issue.

sections.title: The rule every server has to get right
sections.titleHtml: The rule every server has to get right
sections.html:
When a client sends RCPT TO:<someone@example.org>, the server asks one question: is this recipient mine?

  • Yes, the domain is one this server hosts: accept it. This is mail arriving for your users, and it may come from anyone.
  • No, the domain belongs to someone else: accept it only from a client you trust, or from one of your users who has signed in. Otherwise refuse.

Passing mail on to another server is called relaying. A server that relays for anyone is an open relay. The internet's mail standards have asked servers not to do this since 1999 (RFC 2505).

Postfix answers the question with a restriction list, evaluated for every RCPT TO. Its default, since Postfix 2.10, is:

smtpd_relay_restrictions = permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, defer_unauth_destination

Read it left to right:

  1. permit_mynetworks: if the client's IP address is in mynetworks, accept.
  2. permit_sasl_authenticated: if the client signed in, accept.
  3. defer_unauth_destination: if the recipient is not ours, refuse.

The first rule that matches decides. A permit ends the list, and nothing after it runs. That one fact is behind most of what follows.

Postfix has a safety net: it refuses to receive mail at all unless one of its restriction lists contains a rejecting rule, such as reject_unauth_destination or defer_unauth_destination (postconf: smtpd_relay_restrictions). The net checks that a rejecting rule exists. It cannot check that a permit placed before it will never match a stranger.

sections.title: Four ways tutorials break it
sections.html:
Most self-hosted mail servers are assembled from tutorials. Each one copies a different set of lines, often written for an older Postfix, and each fixes the problem in front of it. These four mistakes come up again and again.

1. mynetworks that trusts too much

permit_mynetworks exists so that machines on your own network can send without signing in. A typical story: an application on another server cannot send mail, a guide says to add its network to mynetworks, and the quickest change that works is:

mynetworks = 0.0.0.0/0

That trusts every IPv4 address on the internet. Wider-than-intended ranges do the same thing more quietly: a whole cloud provider's private range, or mynetworks_style = class, which Postfix itself warns "may cause Postfix to 'trust' your entire provider's network" (postconf: mynetworks_style).

The default is safe in modern Postfix: since 3.0, mynetworks_style defaults to host, trusting only the machine itself. But only at compatibility_level = 2 or higher. A server upgraded from an older release often keeps a lower level, and with it the old subnet default, which trusts every machine on the same network (COMPATIBILITY_README).

2. A gateway that makes every client look local

permit_mynetworks judges a client by its IP address. When something forwards connections to Postfix, Postfix can see the forwarder's address instead of the real client's:

  • Docker with IPv6: an IPv6 connection to a container that only has an IPv4 address is forwarded by Docker's userland proxy, and arrives from the network's gateway address (for example 172.17.0.1). docker-mailserver warns that trusting the Docker network "can create an open relay, for instance if IPv6 is enabled on the host machine" (docker-mailserver: PERMIT_DOCKER, IPv6).
  • A TCP proxy or load balancer in front of Postfix, without the PROXY protocol, makes every connection come from the proxy.
  • Kubernetes services do the same by default: with the default externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster, "the source IP seen in the target container is not the original source IP of the client" (Kubernetes: preserving the client source IP).

Tutorials for containers often add the container network to mynetworks, so that other containers can send mail. Combine that with any of the above, and everyone on the internet arrives looking like a trusted local machine.

The fix is to give Postfix the real address, with smtpd_upstream_proxy_protocol = haproxy behind a proxy (postconf), and never to trust a gateway's address.

3. A permit before the reject

Before Postfix 2.10, relay control and spam filtering shared one list, smtpd_recipient_restrictions, which Postfix's own documentation calls "error-prone configuration" (postconf: smtpd_relay_restrictions). Any permit placed before reject_unauth_destination lets a stranger through.

Postfix's documentation gives a real example (SMTPD_ACCESS_README):

smtpd_recipient_restrictions =
    permit_mynetworks
    check_helo_access hash:/etc/postfix/helo_access
    reject_unknown_helo_hostname
    reject_unauth_destination

# /etc/postfix/helo_access
localhost.localdomain PERMIT

The exception was meant for one machine that greets with HELO localhost.localdomain. But anyone can send that greeting, and in their words this makes Postfix "an open relay for all such hosts".

Postfix 2.10 separated the two lists, so this can no longer happen by accident. But for servers migrating from older versions, the documentation allows setting smtpd_relay_restrictions empty and using smtpd_recipient_restrictions "exactly as before". Tutorials that copy that line bring the old trap back.

4. A stolen password and no limits

permit_sasl_authenticated is correct: your users sign in and send. The trouble starts when a password leaks, through phishing, reuse or guessing. From then on, a spammer is one of your users.

Postfix does not limit how much a signed-in user sends. Its rate limits are per client address, and off by default: smtpd_client_message_rate_limit defaults to 0, meaning "a client can send as many message delivery requests per time unit as Postfix can accept" (postconf). A spammer spreading over many addresses is not slowed at all. Limiting per account needs a separate policy service, which most tutorials leave out.

sections.title: Why age makes it worse
sections.html:
None of these mistakes is a bug in Postfix. Postfix is carefully built and well documented. The trouble is that every safer default had to be added on top of older behaviour, without breaking the servers already running it:

  • Safer defaults arrive behind a switch. mynetworks_style = host is the default only at compatibility_level = 2 or higher. An upgraded server keeps the older, wider default until someone raises the level by hand (COMPATIBILITY_README).
  • The old shape stays supported. Setting smtpd_relay_restrictions empty brings back the pre-2.10 combined list, "exactly as before" (postconf).
  • Tutorials outlive the versions they were written for, and are copied into new servers years later.
  • Every protection added since (encryption, sign-in, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS) is another daemon or setting with its own syntax, each with mistakes of its own. Part 2 of this guide goes through them one at a time.

So a server can follow its documentation, start without a warning, and still relay for strangers. REST Mail starts from the other end. It is one modern stack in which the safe behaviour is the only behaviour. Compatibility lives at the edge, where it still speaks SMTP, IMAP and POP3 to everyone, not in a configuration file that carries every old default forward.

sections.title: What it costs
sections.html:
Its source is open-relay-cost.workflow.json.

  • Blocklists. Large mailbox providers and blocklist operators such as Spamhaus see spam from your address, and list it.
  • Your real mail bounces. Servers that check those lists refuse mail from your address, so your users' ordinary mail is rejected with 550 5.7.1 until you are delisted, which happens only after the server is cleaned up.
  • Your host steps in. Hosting providers block port 25 or suspend servers that send spam.
  • Backscatter. Spam sent with forged senders bounces back to those senders, innocent people who never sent anything (BACKSCATTER_README).

sections.title: How to check your own server
sections.titleHtml: How to check your own server
sections.html:
From a machine outside your network, try to relay through your server:

swaks --server mail.example.com --from test@example.net --to someone@gmail.com

A correct server refuses the recipient with 454 4.7.1 (the default defer_unauth_destination) or 554 5.7.1 (reject_unauth_destination), both with "Relay access denied". If it answers 250, it is an open relay.

On the server, read what is actually in effect:

postconf -n mynetworks mynetworks_style compatibility_level smtpd_relay_restrictions smtpd_recipient_restrictions

Check that mynetworks lists only addresses you control, that no permit comes before the rejecting rule, and that a growing queue (postqueue -p) is not your first sign of trouble.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
REST Mail removes the decision that goes wrong, rather than asking you to configure it correctly:

  • No trusted networks. On port 25, REST Mail accepts a recipient only if it is a mailbox it hosts; any other recipient is refused with 550 5.1.1, whatever the client's address. There is no mynetworks to widen. Repeated misses slow the client down. (internal/gateway/smtp/session.go, Rcpt)
  • Relaying only for users who signed in, on the submission port, 465, with TLS from the first byte. MAIL FROM without a login is refused with 530. (session.go, server.go)
  • A real address behind a proxy. REST Mail reads the client's address through the PROXY protocol, only from proxies listed as trusted. Even then, an address never grants relaying. (proxyproto.go)
  • Limits per account, on by default. Each signed-in account has a sending rate limit (451 4.7.1 when exceeded, #171), at most 100 recipients per message, and may only send from addresses it owns (550 otherwise). The REST API's send path has the same limits (#184). These are two of the defences Spamhaus recommends to every mail service: "default per-account limits on numbers of outgoing emails", and "disallowing sending from domains whose mail you do not host" (Spamhaus, 2024).

The trade-off: an application that wants to send through REST Mail signs in with an app password, instead of being trusted for its address.

chapters.title: The black hole: how mail is silently lost
chapters.part: How it goes wrong
chapters.summary: The places a message can disappear without a bounce or an error, why silent loss is worse than any failure you can see, and how to find where it went.
chapters.intro:
Email has always promised one thing above all: a message is either delivered, or the sender is told it was not. A bounce is annoying, but it is honest. The sender knows to try again, or to pick up the phone.

The worst failure is the one that breaks that promise. The message is accepted, everyone believes it arrived, and it is never seen again. Nobody gets an error, so nobody looks for one. RFC 5321 is blunt about it: dropping mail without telling the sender "is extremely dangerous and violates a long tradition and community expectations that mail is either delivered or returned" (§6.2).

We have not found a reliable measurement of how much mail is lost this way. By its nature, it is the failure nobody reports.

The diagram's source is black-hole.workflow.json.

sections.title: Why it happens: responsibility after the 250
sections.titleHtml: Why it happens: responsibility after the 250
sections.html:
The moment a receiving server answers 250 to a message, it takes responsibility for it (The journey of a message). The sender's server deletes its copy. From then on, if the message is lost, there is only one server that can say so, and it is the one that lost it.

So every black hole is a server that accepted a message and then did not deliver it or bounce it. Here are the usual places.

sections.title: On the way: the wrong server says yes
sections.titleHtml: On the way: the wrong server says yes
sections.html:
• An old MX still answering. After a move to a new server, the DNS still lists the old one, or some senders have it cached. The old server is still running, accepts the mail, and stores it in a mailbox nobody reads any more.
  • A catch-all that goes nowhere: a server configured to accept mail for any address at the domain, and deliver what it does not recognise to a mailbox nobody checks, or to nothing.
  • A misconfigured relay or gateway in front of the real server (a spam filtering service, a load balancer) that accepts mail it cannot pass on.

sections.title: On the receiving server: accepted, then dropped
sections.titleHtml: On the receiving server: accepted, then dropped
sections.html:
• Filters that discard. A spam or virus filter that runs after the 250 and deletes what it does not like. The alternative, rejecting during the conversation, makes the sender's server tell the sender (Spam defences).
  • A quarantine nobody reviews. Held for an administrator who never looks, and expired after a month.
  • The spam folder. Technically delivered; in practice, for many readers, never seen.
  • A full mailbox, or an error writing it, handled by dropping instead of bouncing or retrying.
  • Rules the user forgot: a Sieve discard, or a filter that files mail from one sender into a folder nobody opens.

sections.title: Forwarding: accepted, then lost downstream
sections.html: Forwarding adds a second hop after the 250. When the forward fails (the next server rejects it for failing SPF or DMARC, see SPF), the forwarding server must bounce to the original sender (RFC 5321 §6.1). Many forwarders do not, and the message is gone.

sections.title: Bounces that are lost
sections.html:
A bounce is itself a message, sent with an empty envelope sender (Bounces, queues and retries). It can be lost too:

  • Sent to the wrong place, because the original envelope sender was not a real address: a noreply@ that rejects everything.
  • Refused by the sender's own server, because it treats mail from <> as spam. RFC 5321 expects servers to accept it: DSNs and similar notifications "are required by existing and proposed Standards to be sent with a null reverse-path" (§4.5.5).
  • Filed as spam, because bounces look like backscatter.
  • Never generated, because the queue gave up without one.

sections.title: How to find a lost message
sections.titleHtml: How to find a lost message
sections.html:
• Ask the sender for the Message-ID, the time and the recipient, then search the logs of every server on the path. Postfix logs one line per step with a queue ID (status=sent, status=deferred, status=bounced); grep for the Message-ID first, then follow the queue ID.
  • Read the Received: lines of a copy that did arrive somewhere, for the path it took (The journey of a message).
  • DMARC aggregate reports show how many messages from your domain each large receiver saw, and what it did with them (DMARC). A sudden gap is a lead.
  • Check every MX the domain has ever had, and its cached TTL.

sections.title: What a server can do about it
sections.titleHtml: What a server can do about it
sections.html:
• Decide before the 250. Every check that can run during the conversation should: recipients, policy, spam and virus scanning. A refusal is honest.
  • Never discard what you have accepted, except for mail that is clearly fraudulent, as RFC 5321 §6.2 allows, and record it when you do.
  • Make held mail visible: quarantines with notifications, spam folders the user is reminded of.
  • Bounce what cannot be delivered, to the envelope sender, from <>.
  • Keep a trace of every message's fate, so "where did it go?" has an answer.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Checks run before the 250. Unknown recipients are refused during the conversation, and the inbound pipeline runs on the message before it is answered, so a rejection reaches the sender's server as a refusal (internal/gateway/smtp/session.go).
  • No catch-all. A recipient is either a mailbox or an alias REST Mail hosts, or it is refused.
  • Every message has a trace: each delivery records which filters ran, what each decided, and the final outcome (delivered, queued, rejected, quarantined, discarded, deferred), readable through the admin API (internal/api/handlers/trace.go). A discard, by a filter or by the user's own Sieve rule, is recorded, not silent.
  • Quarantine is reported: each user gets a periodic digest of mail held for them (internal/digest/).
  • Bounces for REST Mail's own users go straight into their inbox; a sender elsewhere, whose mail a forward failed to deliver, is sent one by mail (#715).
  • Not yet right: mail to a domain that does not exist is retried for days instead of failing at once (#713), and the queue gives up after 3 days rather than the 4–5 RFC 5321 expects (#711).

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• RFC 5321: §4.5.5 (null reverse-path), §6.1 (reliable delivery), §6.2 (unwanted messages and silent dropping).
  • REST Mail: internal/api/handlers/trace.go, internal/pipeline/, internal/gateway/queue/.

chapters.title: Why the security layers are so hard to get right
chapters.part: How it goes wrong
chapters.summary: Each protection was added on its own, decades apart, by different people, in different places. Here is everything one domain needs, and why mistakes go unnoticed.
chapters.intro:
Each chapter of Part 2 explains one protection, and each one, on its own, is manageable. The trouble is that a domain needs all of them at once, and they were never designed together. They were added one at a time over twenty years, each to fix the problem in front of it, each with its own record, its own syntax, its own software, and its own way of failing.

A 2023 study of email security across the top 10 million domains summed up the result as "grim yet slightly improving" (Blechschmidt and Stock, USENIX Security 2023).

The diagram's source is domain-needs.tree.json.

sections.title: Many layers, added decades apart
sections.html:
Year Layer Standard
1982 SMTP: no encryption, no authentication RFC 821
1999 STARTTLS, and sign-in for sending RFC 2487, RFC 2554
2006 SPF (experimental; standard in 2014) RFC 4408, RFC 7208
2007 DKIM (revised 2011) RFC 4871, RFC 6376
2015 DMARC (informational) RFC 7489
2015 DANE for SMTP RFC 7672
2018 MTA-STS and TLS-RPT RFC 8461, RFC 8460
2019 ARC (experimental) RFC 8617
2026 DMARC as a standard RFC 9989

Every one of them had to work with the mail system as it already was, without breaking any server that did not know about it yet. So each is optional, each is checked separately, and each fails in its own way.

sections.title: Many places, many owners
sections.html:
For one domain to send and receive mail that other servers trust, these all have to be right at the same time:

  • In the domain's DNS: MX, A and AAAA records, an SPF record, a DKIM key for each selector, a DMARC record, the MTA-STS and TLS-RPT records, SRV and autoconfig records for mail apps, and TLSA records if it uses DANE.
  • Somewhere else: the reverse DNS (PTR) record, set by whoever owns the IP address, usually the hosting provider; DNSSEC, which also needs a record at the registrar.
  • On web servers: the MTA-STS policy file at mta-sts.<domain>, and the autoconfig file, each over HTTPS with its own certificate.
  • In certificates: one valid for the MX name, for submission, for IMAP, for mta-sts., for autoconfig., renewed every few months.
  • In keys: DKIM private keys, rotated, with the old selector kept until mail signed with it has arrived.
  • In software: in the classic stack, a different program for each job. One Postfix and Dovecot installation commonly adds OpenDKIM, OpenDMARC, Rspamd or SpamAssassin, ClamAV, Postgrey and Fail2ban, as the bundles in Containers and bundles show. Each has its own configuration file and syntax.
  • In reports: DMARC and TLS-RPT reports, arriving daily, as XML and JSON attachments, to be read by someone.

Often these belong to different people: the DNS to one team, the IP address to the hosting provider, the web server to another team, the certificates to an automation nobody remembers setting up.

sections.title: Mistakes are quiet
sections.html:
What makes the layers truly hard is not their number. It is that almost every mistake is silent where it is made, and shows up somewhere else, later:

  • A broken SPF record (eleven lookups, or two records) does not stop your server sending. It makes other servers distrust your mail, sometimes, by an amount you cannot see.
  • A DKIM key deleted too early fails only the mail in transit, and only at receivers that check.
  • An expired certificate on mta-sts. changes nothing until senders' cached policies expire, weeks later.
  • A missing PTR record shows up as a few providers junking your mail, while others deliver it.
  • A DMARC record at p=reject costs nothing until a user posts to a mailing list (DMARC).

The feedback, when there is any, arrives as a bounce days later, a report nobody reads, or a user saying "they never got my email". The 2023 study found the same at scale: 30% of MX certificates invalid, only about 40% of domains publishing SPF, and DKIM and DANE "neither [...] validated or enforced by all providers" (Blechschmidt and Stock, 2023).

sections.title: Tutorials make it worse
sections.html: Most mail servers are built by following a tutorial, and each tutorial covers the layers that existed when it was written, in the syntax of the software versions it used. A server built from a 2014 guide has no MTA-STS; one built from a 2008 guide may have no DKIM. Each later guide adds a layer on top, in a different style. The open relay and the spam machine shows how that goes wrong for relaying; it goes wrong the same way for every layer here.

sections.title: What would make it easier
sections.html:
Not fewer protections: each one closes a real hole. What helps is having one place that knows all of them:

  • One list of every record a domain needs, generated, not copied from a tutorial, and checked against what is actually published.
  • Keys and certificates made, rotated and renewed automatically, with the DNS changes they need published in the right order.
  • One program doing the jobs, so the protections are configured together, in one way.
  • Reports read by software, and turned into plain warnings.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
REST Mail is built around that list:

  • One server, one configuration. SMTP, IMAP, POP3, signing, checking and filtering are one program behind one REST API, not a stack of daemons (What REST Mail does differently).
  • Records generated and checked: chore dns:show prints the A, MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC and PTR records each domain needs, from the server's own state, and chore dns:check compares them with what is published (internal/dns/mail_records.go), with the SRV records clients find the server by (#712). The DMARC record asks for the domain's own policy, p=none for a new domain, raised by an admin once the reports show its mail passes (#729). Not yet included: MTA-STS and TLS-RPT (#727, #726).
  • Keys made for you: each domain's DKIM key is generated at 2048 bits and stored encrypted; automatic rotation is #728.
  • Certificates renewed with ACME, and reloaded without a restart.
  • Reports read: DMARC reports are sent and TLS-RPT reports received by the server itself; the gaps are in #726 and #730.

sections.title: Sources
sections.html:
• Blechschmidt and Stock: Extended Hell(o), USENIX Security 2023.
  • The RFCs in the table above.
  • REST Mail: internal/dns/, internal/outbound/, internal/acme/.

chapters.title: Deliverability: reputation, warm-up, and why big providers distrust small servers
chapters.part: How it goes wrong
chapters.summary: Why a correctly configured server's mail can still land in spam, how mailbox providers judge a sender, and what a new server can do about it.
chapters.intro:
You set up a mail server, publish every record in this guide, and pass every test. Then your first message to a friend at Gmail lands in their spam folder, and one to Outlook.com is refused outright. Nothing is misconfigured.

This is the part of running a mail server that frustrates people most, and it is not a protocol problem. It is a trust problem. The large mailbox providers receive billions of messages a day, about half of them spam (Spam defences), and they decide what to accept largely on reputation: what they have seen from your address and your domain before. A new server has none.

The diagram's source is reputation.workflow.json.

sections.title: What a provider looks at
sections.html:
Every large provider has its own system, and none publishes all of it. What they do publish, in their sender guidelines, points at the same few things:

  • The sending address (IP). Is it on a blocklist? Is it a home or cloud address that should not send mail directly? Does it have reverse DNS that matches? What has it sent before, and did people want it?
  • The domain. The From: domain and the DKIM signing domain carry their own reputation, which follows the domain from server to server. That is why authentication matters: it lets a provider attach reputation to a name you control rather than only to an address.
  • Authentication: SPF, DKIM and DMARC, aligned (DMARC).
  • How recipients react: spam reports, mail deleted unread, mail moved out of the spam folder. Gmail asks senders to keep spam reports below 0.3% (Google, Email sender guidelines).
  • The content and its formatting, last.

sections.title: Why small servers start behind
sections.html:
• No history. A new address has sent nothing, so a provider has nothing good to weigh against the risk of a sender it does not know.
  • Addresses that should not send mail directly. Spamhaus's Policy Blocklist lists "end-user IP address ranges from which email should never be sent directly to the final destination", often "ranges assigned by ISPs to broadband or dial-up customers" (Spamhaus, PBL). A server at home is almost certainly on it.
  • Cloud neighbours. An address from a cloud provider's pool may have been used by a spammer last month. Many cloud providers block outgoing port 25 altogether by default: "By default, Amazon EC2 allows outbound traffic over port 25 only to private IPv4 addresses" (AWS), and on Google Cloud "connections to destination TCP Port 25 are blocked when the destination is external to your VPC network" (Google Cloud).
  • Low volume. A server that sends a few messages a day never builds the statistics a provider uses to trust it, and one spam report weighs heavily among few messages.

None of this is unfair to small servers on purpose. It is the cost of an open system where anyone can send, and most of those who try are spammers.

sections.title: Building a reputation
sections.html:
• A clean, dedicated address with matching forward and reverse DNS, from a provider that allows mail, and not on any blocklist: check it before you start.
  • Every authentication layer from day one: SPF, DKIM, DMARC at p=none with reports, TLS.
  • Warm up. Google's advice is to "Increase sending volume slowly to avoid delivery problems", and that "The more email that you send, the more slowly you should increase sending volume". If messages start being deferred, "reduce the sending volume until the SMTP error rate decreases" (Google, Email sender guidelines).
  • Keep kinds of mail apart. The same guidelines suggest "a different IP address for each message type. For example, use one IP address for sending account notifications and a different IP address for sending promotional messages", so a newsletter's complaints do not hold up password resets.
  • Stop sending to addresses that bounce, and to people who complain: "Automatically unsubscribe recipients who have multiple bounced messages", and "Don't purchase email addresses from other companies" (the same page).
  • Use the providers' own tools: Google Postmaster Tools shows Gmail's view of your domain's spam rate and reputation, and Microsoft's Smart Network Data Services shows Outlook.com's view of your addresses. Outlook.com's own words: "Deliverability to Outlook.com is based on your reputation."
  • Join feedback loops, where providers send you a report each time a recipient marks your mail as spam (RFC 5965 defines the format).

sections.title: When you are blocked
sections.html: The refusal message usually says why, and where to go: a blocklist's name and lookup page, or a provider's sender support form. Fix the cause first (a compromised account, an open relay, a missing record), then ask for delisting. Delisting before the cause is fixed only gets you listed again.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Authentication from the start: every message DKIM-signed; SPF, DMARC and PTR records printed for each domain; TLS whenever the receiver offers it.
  • Your own address, watched: REST Mail can check its sending addresses against DNS blocklists on a schedule and report a listing in its logs and metrics, so you hear before your users do (docs/dnsbl-monitor.md).
  • Limits per account: a stolen login cannot send thousands of messages and burn the server's reputation in an afternoon (Who may send).
  • Hard bounces remembered: an address that bounces with "no such mailbox" is not sent to again for 90 days.
  • Bulk and transactional kept apart: a domain can be marked bulk or transactional, and the send API holds it to that (Bulk mail).
  • Not yet: feedback-loop complaints are not processed (#733), and there is no built-in warm-up schedule.

sections.html:
