chapters.title: The servers compared: Postfix, Exim, Dovecot, Stalwart, and the hosted services
chapters.part: The landscape, and where REST Mail fits
chapters.summary: The jobs a mail server does, the programs that do them, from the classic one-job daemons to all-in-one servers and hosted services, and what each does well.
chapters.intro:
There is no single "mail server". There are jobs (moving mail between servers, storing it, serving it to apps, signing it, checking it, filtering it) and programs that do one or several of them. Most of the internet's mail runs on a handful of mature open-source programs, combined; a newer generation does all the jobs in one; and much of the world's mail is handled by a few hosted services that do all of it for you.

This chapter describes each in its own terms. Every one of them has served people well, and many of the fixes this guide explains were first written in them.

The diagram's source is servers.tree.json.

sections.title: The jobs
sections.html:
Job What it does Protocol
Transfer (MTA) Receives mail from other servers, queues and delivers outgoing mail SMTP
Submission Takes mail from your users' apps, with sign-in SMTP, port 465/587
Storage and access Keeps mailboxes, serves them to apps, runs Sieve rules IMAP, POP3, JMAP
Authentication Signs outgoing mail, checks SPF, DKIM, DMARC and ARC on incoming DNS, crypto
Filtering Spam and virus scanning, greylisting, blocklists various
Administration Domains, mailboxes, aliases, passwords, keys, certificates files, SQL, LDAP, web

sections.title: Transfer agents
sections.html:
• Postfix is "Wietse Venema's mail server that started life at IBM research as an alternative to the widely-used Sendmail program", and "attempts to be fast, easy to administer, and secure" (postfix.org). It is built as a set of small cooperating programs, one per step: smtpd receives, cleanup checks, qmgr queues, smtp delivers (Postfix architecture overview). Its documentation is thorough, and much of it is quoted in this guide.
  • Exim "is a message transfer agent (MTA) originally developed at the University of Cambridge [...] There is a great deal of flexibility in the way mail can be routed, and there are extensive facilities for checking incoming mail" (exim.org). DKIM is built in; SPF and DMARC are options when Exim is compiled, using libspf2 and libopendmarc (Exim: DKIM, SPF, SRS and DMARC).
  • Sendmail is the program Postfix and Exim were written to replace; "Exim can be installed in place of Sendmail" (exim.org). Its open-source version is maintained by Proofpoint (Proofpoint).
  • OpenSMTPD "is a FREE implementation of the server-side SMTP protocol as defined by RFC 5321", "Started out of dissatisfaction with other implementations", from the OpenBSD project (opensmtpd.org). Its configuration is short and readable.
  • Haraka "is an open source SMTP server written in Node.js which provides extremely high performance coupled with a flexible plugin system" (haraka.github.io). Every step of the conversation can be hooked by a plugin, which makes it popular as a filtering front end.

sections.title: Mailbox servers
sections.html:
• Dovecot is "the world's most trusted open-source email server", in its own words "Powering over 75% of the World's Email Servers", first released in 2002 (dovecot.org). It serves IMAP and POP3, stores mail, runs Sieve (through Pigeonhole), and usually takes delivery from Postfix or Exim over LMTP. It also answers sign-in questions for them.
  • Cyrus IMAP "is an email, contacts and calendar server", with replication, CalDAV and CardDAV (cyrusimap.org), and is one of the JMAP servers (jmap.io).

sections.title: Signing and filtering, alongside
sections.html: The classic transfer agents leave signing and most checking to separate programs connected through the milter interface: OpenDKIM and OpenDMARC for DKIM and DMARC, an SPF policy service, Rspamd or SpamAssassin for spam, ClamAV for viruses, Postgrey for greylisting, Fail2ban for repeated failed sign-ins. This is flexible, and each piece is good at its job; it is also why a working server is a set of programs to configure, connect and keep current (Why the security layers are so hard).

sections.title: All in one
sections.html:
A newer generation does every job in one program, with one configuration:

  • Stalwart, written in Rust: "Secure, scalable mail & collaboration server with comprehensive protocol support (IMAP, JMAP, SMTP, CalDAV, CardDAV, WebDAV)", with DKIM, SPF, DMARC, ARC, DANE, MTA-STS and spam filtering built in (Stalwart). It is dual-licensed, AGPL-3.0 or a commercial licence.
  • Maddy, written in Go: it "replaces Postfix, Dovecot, OpenDKIM, OpenSPF, OpenDMARC and more with one daemon with uniform configuration and minimal maintenance cost", though its maintainers note that "IMAP storage is "beta"" (Maddy).

sections.title: Hosted services
sections.html:
• Microsoft 365 (Exchange Online) and Google Workspace (Gmail) run the whole stack for you: servers, storage, filtering, authentication, apps, and the reputation of very large sending networks. You manage users and DNS records, and what the admin console allows. The trade-offs are a per-user price, your mail on their servers under their terms, and proprietary systems you cannot inspect or change. Both also apply the sender rules every other server has to meet (Bulk mail).
  • Exchange Server is Microsoft's on-premises server, for organisations that run their own.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.html:
Language Transfer Storage and access Signing and checking built in Filtering built in
Postfix C yes no no (milters) some (postscreen)
Exim C yes no DKIM; SPF and DMARC as build options ACLs
OpenSMTPD C yes no no (filters) filters
Haraka JavaScript yes no plugins plugins
Dovecot C no IMAP, POP3, Sieve no no
Cyrus IMAP C no IMAP, POP3, JMAP, Sieve no no
Stalwart Rust yes IMAP, POP3, JMAP yes yes
Maddy Go yes IMAP (beta) yes some
REST Mail Go yes IMAP, POP3, REST API yes yes

Languages are as GitHub reports them for each project's repository.

sections.title: How REST Mail fits
sections.html:
REST Mail is in the all-in-one group: one program behind one REST API does transfer, submission, storage, access, signing, checking and filtering (What REST Mail does differently). It differs from the others in three ways:

  • The REST API is the server. SMTP, IMAP and POP3 are gateways in front of it, and REST Mail's own apps use the API directly.
  • It is built to be safe without configuration, so that the open relay and the black hole cannot be configured in (The open relay).
  • It is still young. The projects above have years or decades of production use; this guide links every place where REST Mail does not yet do what the RFCs ask.

sections.html:

chapters.title: Containers and bundles: what packaging solves, and what stays the same
chapters.part: The landscape, and where REST Mail fits
chapters.summary: How docker-mailserver, mailcow, Mailu, Mail-in-a-Box, iRedMail and kubernetes-mail-server package the classic stack, what that makes easier, and what is still inside.
chapters.intro:
Building a mail server from a tutorial means installing and connecting a dozen programs by hand (Why the security layers are so hard). A family of projects does that work once, well, and hands you the result: a set of containers, or a script that turns a fresh machine into a mail server. They have made running your own mail possible for many people who would otherwise not have tried, and several of the warnings quoted in this guide come from their documentation.

REST Mail's author built two of these: a Docker-based mail server, and kubernetes-mail-server. This chapter draws on that experience: what packaging solves, and what stays the same inside the package.

The diagram's source is bundle.workflow.json.

sections.title: The bundles
sections.html:
Each describes itself, and what it includes, in its own documentation:

  • docker-mailserver: "A production-ready fullstack but simple containerized mail server (SMTP, IMAP, LDAP, Anti-spam, Anti-virus, etc.)", with "Only configuration files, no SQL database". It includes Postfix, Dovecot, Rspamd, Amavis, SpamAssassin, ClamAV, OpenDKIM, OpenDMARC, Fail2ban, Postscreen, Postgrey, Fetchmail and Getmail6, in one container.
  • mailcow: dockerized: a suite of containers. Its Compose file defines eighteen services, among them Postfix, Dovecot, Rspamd, ClamAV, SOGo, MariaDB, Redis, Nginx, Unbound and an ACME client (docker-compose.yml).
  • Mailu: "a simple yet full-featured mail server as a set of Docker images", with images for Postfix, Dovecot, Rspamd, Nginx and an admin interface, and optional ones for Fetchmail, Radicale and Unbound.
  • Mail-in-a-Box: "turns a fresh Ubuntu 22.04 LTS 64-bit machine into a working mail server by installing and configuring various components": Postfix, Dovecot, Nextcloud, Z-Push, Roundcube, SpamAssassin, Postgrey, nsd4, OpenDKIM, Let's Encrypt, duplicity, ufw, Fail2ban and Munin. It sets SPF, DKIM, DMARC, DNSSEC, DANE TLSA and MTA-STS records automatically, and is deliberately not customisable: "There are no user-configurable setup options. It "just works.""
  • iRedMail: "a full-featured mail server solution" installed onto a supported Linux or BSD system, with accounts in OpenLDAP, MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL, and "SpamAssassin, ClamAV, SPF, DKIM, greylisting", Roundcube or SOGo for webmail.
  • kubernetes-mail-server: "A dovecot/postfix/opendkim/mysql Email Server which runs on Kubernetes", with one repository and image per component: Postfix, Dovecot, OpenDKIM, Rspamd, ClamAV, Redis, the database, and a setup job.

sections.title: What packaging solves
sections.html:
• Installation. A working server in an afternoon instead of a week.
  • Known-good defaults. The pieces are connected the same way every time, by people who have fixed the mistakes before. Many of the tutorial errors in The open relay cannot happen with an up-to-date bundle.
  • Upgrades. A new image replaces every component at once, tested together.
  • The supporting work: certificates, DNS records to publish, an admin interface, backups, health checks, depending on the bundle.

sections.title: What stays the same
sections.html:
Underneath, it is the same classic stack: an MTA, a mailbox server, and a program for each check, each with its own configuration language. Packaging changes who writes that configuration, not whether it exists.

  • The configuration is still there. A bundle generates main.cf, master.cf, dovecot.conf, Rspamd's settings and the rest from its own, simpler settings. When something goes wrong, or you need something the bundle did not foresee, you are back in those files, now with a layer of templates between you and them.
  • The bundle can add its own traps. Containers change how addresses look: docker-mailserver warns that trusting the Docker network "can create an open relay, for instance if IPv6 is enabled on the host machine" (docker-mailserver: PERMIT_DOCKER), and Kubernetes hides client addresses by default (The open relay).
  • Every component still has to be understood to debug it. A message that went missing may have been lost in Postfix, a milter, Rspamd, Dovecot or a Sieve script, each with its own log format.
  • The protocols' limits are unchanged. A bundle cannot make SMTP authenticate senders, or make a forward pass SPF; it can only configure the same add-ons every server uses.
  • Security fixes still depend on every upstream project, and on the bundle releasing a new image in time.

That is the lesson REST Mail's author took from building kubernetes-mail-server: packaging makes the stack easier to install and harder to misconfigure, which is a real improvement. But it wraps the problem rather than removing it. The many programs, configuration languages and failure modes are still inside.

sections.title: Which to choose
sections.html: If you want a mature, widely used stack today, a bundle is the safest way to get one: pick the one whose scope (one container or many, a web interface or none, customisable or not) fits how you work, and follow its documentation rather than a tutorial. Keep it updated.

sections.title: How REST Mail differs
sections.html:
REST Mail is not a bundle. It does not package Postfix and Dovecot; it replaces them with one program, so there is no generated configuration underneath and no set of daemons to keep in step (What REST Mail does differently):

  • No mynetworks, no milters, no main.cf. The behaviours that go wrong in those files are not settings in REST Mail at all.
  • One log and one trace for every message, across every step.
  • One install with Helm or the installer, and one image per release.

It still speaks SMTP, IMAP and POP3 to everyone else, so it can sit beside a bundle during a migration.

chapters.title: Efforts to modernise email: JMAP, end-to-end encryption, and others
chapters.part: The landscape, and where REST Mail fits
chapters.summary: Forty years of attempts to improve email, from new standards inside the system to proposals to replace it, what each solved, where each stands today, and how they relate to REST Mail.
chapters.intro:
Email is older than the web, and almost every part of it has been improved, or someone has tried. Those efforts fall into two kinds: upgrades inside the system, which every server can adopt one at a time while still talking to the rest; and replacements, which ask everyone to change at once. The first kind has mostly succeeded. The second has mostly not, for the same reason email itself has survived: anyone can still send mail to anyone.

The diagram's source is standards.workflow.json.

sections.title: Upgrades inside the system
sections.html:
Security, added one layer at a time. STARTTLS (1999), SPF (2006), DKIM (2007), DMARC (2015), DANE (2015), MTA-STS and TLS-RPT (2018), ARC (2019), and DMARC as a standard in 2026. Each closed a real hole while every server that ignored it kept working. Part 2 of this guide covers each; Why the security layers are so hard covers the cost of having so many.

Cleartext retired. RFC 8314 (2018) declared "Cleartext Considered Obsolete" for mail apps, and the large providers now refuse ordinary passwords from them (Who may send).

Mail for every language. Internationalised email (RFC 6531, 2012, and its companions) allows addresses and headers in any script, so a user need not have an ASCII address at all.

JMAP, a modern protocol for mail apps. RFC 8620 and RFC 8621 (2019) replace IMAP's long-lived connections and many round trips with batched JSON over HTTPS, a "changes since" model and push. It is implemented by Fastmail, Cyrus IMAP, Stalwart, Apache James and others, and by a growing list of apps (jmap.io), but most desktop mail apps still speak only IMAP (Reading mail).

Brand logos: BIMI. Brand Indicators for Message Identification let a domain publish a logo that providers may show beside its mail. It is "a display signal on top of strong authentication": "At a minimum, BIMI requires DMARC alignment, and many providers also require a valid Certificate (VMC or CMC) proving rights to the logo" (BIMI Group). Its value to the system is that it gives brands a reason to move DMARC to enforcement.

sections.title: End-to-end encryption
sections.html:
Everything above protects mail in transit, between servers. The servers themselves can read it. Encrypting it so that only the recipient can read it is an older and harder problem:

  • S/MIME (RFC 8551, version 4.0 in
    1. uses certificates from certificate authorities, and is common inside organisations that issue them.
  • OpenPGP (RFC 9580, revised in
    1. uses keys people manage themselves.
  • Autocrypt "is a set of guidelines for developers to achieve convenient end-to-end-encryption of e-mails", using OpenPGP, in which mail apps exchange keys automatically in ordinary messages (autocrypt.org).
  • Delta Chat builds a messenger on top of email and Autocrypt, with "Audited end-to-end encryption safe against network and server attacks" (delta.chat).

All of them face the same obstacles: finding the recipient's key, managing keys across devices, and the fact that encrypted mail cannot be searched or filtered by the server.

sections.title: Replacements that did not take hold
sections.titleHtml: Replacements that did not take hold
sections.html: • Internet Mail 2000, proposed by D. J. Bernstein, turned delivery around: "Mail storage is the sender's responsibility", and the receiver picks the message up from the sender's server; with each message's delivery status in the sender's own archive, "There's no need for bounces" (cr.yp.to/im2000). It would also require every server and every client to change at once, and it was not adopted. The lesson: a change that works only when everyone adopts it at once is very hard to make on an open system where anyone can still send mail to anyone.

sections.title: Where REST Mail fits
sections.html:
REST Mail is an upgrade inside the system, not a replacement:

  • It speaks SMTP, IMAP and POP3 to everyone, so it can replace one server at a time without anyone else changing.
  • It adopts every in-system standard this guide describes, and tracks where it does not yet: DANE (#725), JMAP (#720), reading DMARC reports (#730).
  • Between two REST Mail servers, it upgrades the delivery itself: the RESTMAIL protocol delivers over HTTPS with verified endpoints, falling back to ordinary SMTP for everyone else. That is the same shape as every successful upgrade before it: better between those who support it, compatible with everyone who does not.

sections.html:

  • jmap.io: software.
  • BIMI Group: FAQs for senders.
  • autocrypt.org, delta.chat.
  • D. J. Bernstein: Internet Mail 2000.

chapters.title: What REST Mail does differently
chapters.part: The landscape, and where REST Mail fits
chapters.summary: One server with a REST API at its centre, protocol gateways in front of it, safe behaviour that is not a setting, and full compatibility with every other mail server and app.
chapters.intro:
Every chapter so far ends with a section on how REST Mail handles its subject. This chapter steps back and shows the design those sections come from.

The short version: REST Mail is one server with a REST API at its centre. SMTP, IMAP and POP3 are gateways in front of that API, so every other server and every mail app sees an ordinary mail server, and REST Mail's own apps, automations and agents use the API directly. The protections in this guide are built into that one program, mostly as behaviour rather than as settings.

The diagram's source is rest-mail.architecture.json.

sections.title: A REST API at the centre
sections.titleHtml: A REST API at the centre
sections.html:
In the classic stack, the mail server is the MTA, and everything else plugs into it (The servers compared). In REST Mail, the server is an HTTP API backed by PostgreSQL: mailboxes, messages, folders, filters, domains, keys and permissions are all resources in it (internal/api/, openapi.yaml).

  • The protocol gateways for SMTP, IMAP and POP3 are thin adapters: each wire protocol is spoken by a library (go-smtp, go-imap, go-pop3), and the gateway turns its commands into API calls (internal/gateway/). A server or a mail app cannot tell REST Mail from any other mail server.
  • REST Mail's own apps (the iPhone app, webmail, admin webmail) use the API directly, with live updates and push notifications.
  • Automations and agents use the same API with their own API keys, under the same permission system as people (internal/auth/api_key.go).

sections.title: Safe behaviour that is not a setting
sections.titleHtml: Safe behaviour that is not a setting
sections.html:
The mistakes in Part 3 mostly come from settings that can be set wrong. REST Mail removes the settings:

In the classic stack In REST Mail
mynetworks decides who may relay Nobody relays without signing in; there is no trusted network to widen
Submission on 587, IMAP on 143, POP3 on 110, with or without TLS Implicit TLS on 465, 993 and 995 only; no setting for the cleartext ports exists
Rate limits off by default, per IP Limits per account, on by default
Any signed-in user may send as anyone, unless configured Only from addresses the account owns, or holds a grant on
DKIM signing through a separate daemon, if configured Every outbound message signed, or held until it can be
DNS records copied from a tutorial Records generated from the server's state, and checked
Mail accepted, then filtered, maybe dropped Filters run before the 250; every outcome traced

sections.title: One pipeline for every check
sections.html: Each domain has an inbound and an outbound pipeline of filters, run in order: SPF, DKIM, DMARC and ARC checks, greylisting, size and rate limits, spam and virus scanning through Rspamd and ClamAV, Sieve, vacation replies, webhooks, and JavaScript filters that run in a sandbox, each in its own QuickJS engine compiled to WebAssembly, with memory and time limits (internal/pipeline/, docs/adapter-filters.md). One configuration, one API, one trace per message.

sections.title: One permission system
sections.html: Everything a person, app or agent may do is a capability, granted on an account or a domain, and checked by the API on every request. Mail apps sign in with app passwords; accounts with two-factor authentication cannot use their own password for IMAP, POP3 or SMTP; administrators switch on full rights only for a while, with a reason, and every administrative action goes into a hash-chained audit log (internal/grants/, internal/audit/).

sections.title: Compatible with everyone
sections.html:
REST Mail is meant to live alongside the servers it improves on:

  • SMTP, IMAP and POP3 to every other server and app. Each protocol library is tested against its RFCs, with a checklist of their requirements; making that checklist complete for every library is #374.
  • Passwords stored in Dovecot's {BLF-CRYPT} format. Importing accounts with the password hashes they already have is planned (Migrating step by step).
  • Between two REST Mail servers, delivery upgrades to HTTPS with the RESTMAIL protocol, and falls back to SMTP for everyone else.
  • Where REST Mail does not yet do what the RFCs ask, this guide links the issue, and the project's rule is to change REST Mail to comply.

sections.title: Libraries anyone can use
sections.html: The protocol and authentication code is split into libraries, each usable on its own, each MIT-licensed: go-smtp (a fork of emersion's), go-imap, go-pop3, go-dkim, go-spf, go-dmarc, go-arc, go-mtasts and go-sieve.

sections.title: What is not done yet
sections.html: REST Mail is young, and this guide is honest about it. The issues linked from its chapters cover, among others: queue lifetimes and timeouts to RFC 5321 (#711, #714), DANE (#725), DMARC to RFC 9989 (#729, #730), DKIM rotation (#728), and JMAP (#720). Solved, solving, still open lists them all.

chapters.title: RESTMAIL: delivery between servers over HTTPS
chapters.part: The landscape, and where REST Mail fits
chapters.summary: How two REST Mail servers find out about each other and deliver over HTTPS instead of SMTP, what that gains, and why it always falls back to ordinary SMTP for everyone else.
chapters.intro:
Every upgrade to email that has succeeded has had the same shape: better between the servers that support it, unchanged for those that do not (Efforts to modernise email). RESTMAIL is REST Mail's upgrade of that shape for delivery itself. When a REST Mail server delivers to another REST Mail server, it can skip the SMTP conversation and post the message over HTTPS. To every other server, it is an ordinary SMTP server.

This is REST Mail's own protocol, not an IETF standard. Its endpoints are part of REST Mail's API description (openapi.yaml).

The diagram's source is restmail.sequence.json.

sections.title: Why HTTPS
sections.html:
SMTP works, everywhere, and RESTMAIL never replaces it for anyone who does not speak RESTMAIL. Between two servers that both do, HTTPS offers what SMTP had to add later, or never got:

  • Encryption is not optional, and cannot be stripped: there is no cleartext offer to delete (Encryption in transit).
  • The server's certificate is always checked, against a name taken from the recipient's MX records, the web's ordinary way, rather than accepted whatever it is.
  • The message travels as it is, in one request, with no dot-stuffing, no line length limits, and no 7-bit history.
  • Ordinary web infrastructure: HTTP libraries, load balancers, logs and tools everyone already has.

sections.title: How it works
sections.html:
1. The hint. REST Mail's SMTP gateway lists an extension called RESTMAIL in its EHLO reply. A sending REST Mail server that sees it on a recipient's MX knows the MX may speak RESTMAIL. The hint arrives in cleartext, so it is only a hint: any address it carries is ignored.
  2. Verified discovery. The sender asks the MX host itself, over HTTPS, where to deliver: GET https://<mx-host>/.well-known/restmail?domain=example.org. The certificate must be valid for the MX host name; redirects are refused; the answer is capped at 4 KiB. The answer names the endpoint: {"endpoint": "https://mail.example.org/restmail"}. A 404 or 410 here is a verified "not hosted": the sender records that, and uses SMTP.
  3. Delivery. The sender posts the message, DKIM-signed as always, to POST <endpoint>/messages, again verifying the certificate.
  4. Acceptance. The receiver accepts the delivery from a trusted peer network, or when the message carries a DKIM signature that verifies and aligns with the From: domain; it refuses an unauthenticated delivery claiming one of its own domains. Then the message goes through the domain's inbound pipeline, exactly as one that arrived by SMTP.

The receiver can also answer whether a mailbox exists (GET /restmail/mailboxes?address=), slowing down each answer for a mailbox that does not, so it cannot be used to collect addresses.

sections.title: Safety rules
sections.html:
• An MTA-STS policy still applies. Under an enforce policy, a sender only asks a discovery host the policy names (MTA-STS).
  • Only the MX host can say where the endpoint is. The cleartext EHLO advertisement cannot redirect mail anywhere (#291).
  • What a sender remembers is only whether an MX speaks REST, and only for that MX host; the endpoint is asked for again on every delivery.

sections.title: What it is not
sections.html:
• Not a replacement for SMTP. Most of the world's servers will never speak it, and REST Mail delivers to them over SMTP, as it receives from them.
  • Not end-to-end encryption. Each server can still read the mail it holds, as with SMTP.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Advertising and discovery: the SMTP gateway advertises RESTMAIL (internal/gateway/smtp/server.go), and the API answers /.well-known/restmail (internal/api/handlers/restmail_discovery.go).
  • Sending: the outbound queue probes, discovers and delivers (internal/gateway/queue/restmail_discovery.go, worker.go).
  • Receiving: deliveries are authenticated before they are accepted (internal/api/handlers/restmail_deliver_auth.go).
  • Fallback today: a RESTMAIL delivery that fails for any reason other than a verified "not hosted" is retried over SMTP. The design decided in #292 goes further: once a server knows a domain runs REST Mail, it uses only REST for it, so an attacker who blocks HTTPS cannot push the mail back to SMTP. That, and protecting the very first contact, are parked until the core mail flow is complete (#292).

chapters.title: Migrating step by step, without breaking anything
chapters.part: The landscape, and where REST Mail fits
chapters.summary: How to move a domain's mail from one server to another while mail keeps flowing, in an order where every step can be undone.
chapters.intro:
Moving a domain to a new mail server is nerve-racking because mail does not stop while you work. Messages arrive at whichever server the sender's DNS cache points to, signatures are checked against whichever keys are published, and mail apps keep connecting to the old settings. The way through is to run both servers side by side, change one thing at a time, and keep every step reversible until the end.

This chapter is written for any move between servers. It applies to moving onto REST Mail, from Postfix and Dovecot or a bundle, and equally to moving away.

The diagram's source is migration.workflow.json.

sections.title: 1. Prepare
sections.html:
• Write down what exists: every domain, mailbox and alias, every forward and Sieve rule, every service that sends as the domain (the website, the newsletter, the invoicing system), the DKIM selectors in use, and the current MX, SPF, DMARC and PTR records.
  • Lower the TTLs. A record's TTL is "the time interval that the resource record may be cached before the source of the information should again be consulted" (RFC 1035 §3.2.1). At least one full old TTL before the cutover, lower the MX and the mail host's A and AAAA records to a few minutes, so the switch takes effect quickly, and can be undone quickly.
  • Get the new server's address right first: a clean IP, with a PTR record that matches its name, not on any blocklist (Deliverability).

sections.title: 2. Run both
sections.html:
• Set up the new server with the domains and mailboxes, but do not point the MX at it yet. It can be tested by connecting to it directly.
  • Publish both servers' keys and addresses. Add the new server's DKIM key under a new selector, beside the old one, so mail signed by either server verifies. Add the new server to the SPF record, alongside the old one. Neither change affects the mail already flowing.
  • Copy the mail while users keep working on the old server. Any IMAP-to-IMAP tool can do it; imapsync is "an IMAP transfer tool" whose "purpose [...] is to migrate IMAP accounts". Run it once now, and again at the cutover to pick up what arrived since.
  • Test: send to and from the new server, check DKIM, SPF and DMARC pass at a large provider, and sign in from a mail app.

sections.title: 3. Cut over
sections.html:
• Point the MX at the new server. With a short TTL, most senders follow within minutes. Some will still use the old MX for a while: keep the old server running and accepting mail, and either have it forward to the new one, or copy its late arrivals across with a final sync.
  • Move the mail apps: update autoconfig and the SRV records (Finding the server), and tell users the new settings, or use a server name that you move with the MX.
  • Watch: DMARC aggregate reports and the new server's logs show any service still sending through the old path, or failing authentication.

If something is badly wrong, point the MX back. Nothing has been removed yet.

sections.title: 4. Retire the old server
sections.html:
Only when nothing has arrived at the old server for several days:

  • Remove the old server from SPF and from any mynetworks or relay setting elsewhere that trusted it.
  • Remove the old DKIM selector, at least a few days after the old server stopped sending, so mail signed with it and still in queues verifies.
  • Raise the TTLs back to normal.
  • Keep the old server's data until you are sure nothing is missing, then shut it down.

sections.title: What goes wrong
sections.html:
• Forgetting a sender: the website's contact form still relays through the old server, which is now gone.
  • Removing the old DKIM key at the cutover, so mail in transit fails.
  • A long TTL, so half the internet delivers to the old server for a day.
  • A final sync that is never run, so mail that arrived at the old server during the cutover is lost: the black hole in its purest form.
  • Turning the old server off first. Keep it accepting until the very end.

sections.title: How REST Mail handles it
sections.html:
• Running both: REST Mail speaks SMTP, IMAP and POP3, so it sits beside any other server for as long as the migration needs, and can be tested directly before the MX changes.
  • The records to publish for each domain, including its DKIM key under its own selector, come from chore dns:show, and chore dns:check shows what is still missing (DNS for email).
  • Mail apps find the new settings by autoconfig and Autodiscover; the settings are implicit TLS on 465 and 993, so apps set up for 587 or 143 need changing.
  • Existing passwords: import an account's ARGON2ID, ARGON2I, BLF-CRYPT, SHA256-CRYPT or SHA512-CRYPT hash with restmail import-account, or a whole Dovecot passwd-file with restmail import-passwd-file, without issuing a new password. See importing accounts for permissions, work-factor limits and the API. SHA-crypt and Argon2 hashes become bcrypt after a matching password proof, when the password fits bcrypt's length limit.
  • Still to come: importing mail from IMAP, Maildir or mbox remains in #734. Mail can be copied over IMAP with a tool such as imapsync; that cutover still needs proof against REST Mail.

sections.html:

chapters.title: Solved, solving, still open
chapters.part: The landscape, and where REST Mail fits
chapters.summary: Every problem in this guide in one table, how far email as a whole has got with it, and where REST Mail stands, with the issue for each gap.
chapters.intro: This is the guide in one place: each problem it describes, whether the email system as a whole has a standard answer, and where REST Mail stands. "Solved" here means a standard exists and is widely deployed, not that every server uses it. Each row links to the chapter that explains it.

sections.title: Delivery
sections.html:
Problem Email as a whole REST Mail
Open relays Solved by default in modern MTAs; brought back by configuration mistakes No trusted networks; relaying only after sign-in
Stolen logins sending spam Still open: limits per account are not a default in the classic stack Per-account limits on by default; complaints not yet processed (#733)
Finding the MX Solved Implicit and null MX handled; a domain that does not exist is retried instead of failing (#713)
Retrying for long enough Solved (RFC 5321: 4–5 days) Gives up after 3 days (#711); one timeout for the whole attempt (#714)
Backscatter Solved where servers refuse during the conversation Refuses during the conversation
Silently lost mail Still open: depends on every server's behaviour Traces every outcome; failed forwards bounced to the original sender (#715); vacation replies to <> (#716)
SMTP smuggling Being solved: Postfix, for example, shipped fixes in 2023–2024 (Postfix) Only CRLF ends a line

sections.title: Encryption
sections.html:
Problem Email as a whole REST Mail
Mail readable on the wire Mostly solved: 98–99% of Gmail's outbound mail is encrypted STARTTLS on 25; implicit TLS everywhere else
Delivery to servers with bad certificates Solved by opportunistic TLS Opportunistic: encrypts, and records the certificate as unverified (#723)
STARTTLS downgrade Being solved: MTA-STS and DANE, adopted slowly MTA-STS enforced when sending; the _mta-sts record printed with an id that follows the policy, the mta-sts. host and its certificate not yet (#727); no DANE (#725)
Hearing about TLS failures Solved by TLS-RPT, where published Receives reports over HTTPS; does not send them (#726)
Encryption required per message Standard exists (REQUIRETLS), little deployed TLS-Required: No honoured; REQUIRETLS not supported yet (#724)
End-to-end encryption Still open: S/MIME and OpenPGP exist; key discovery remains hard Not addressed

sections.title: Authentication
sections.html:
Problem Email as a whole REST Mail
Who may send for a domain Solved by SPF Checked on HELO and MAIL FROM; v=spf1 mx -all recommended
Proving a message's origin Solved by DKIM Every message signed; keys not yet rotated automatically (#728)
Forged From: lines Solved by DMARC, now an IETF standard (RFC 9989) Applied, to RFC 9989; reports sent to RFC 9990, not yet read (#730); a new domain starts at p=none
Forwarding and mailing lists Being solved: ARC, experimental, used by large providers Verifies ARC, and seals the mail it forwards (#731)
Passwords in mail apps Being solved: app passwords and OAuth App passwords; no OAuth

sections.title: Reading and setup
sections.html:
Problem Email as a whole REST Mail
Mail on every device Solved by IMAP; JMAP for mobile and web IMAP4rev1 and its key extensions, SPECIAL-USE, and most of IMAP4rev2's; IMAP4rev2 itself (#718) and JMAP (#720) not yet
Server-side rules Solved by Sieve and ManageSieve Sieve; no ManageSieve (#719)
Mail app setup Being solved: autoconfig is an IETF draft; SRV records Autoconfig and Autodiscover, with two bugs (#721, #722); SRV records (#712)

sections.title: Operating a server
sections.html:
Problem Email as a whole REST Mail
Too many separate layers Still open: each layer is configured separately One program; records generated and checked
New servers distrusted Still open: reputation has to be earned Authentication from day one; blocklist monitor for its own addresses
Bulk mail rules Solved, and enforced since 2024–2025 One-click unsubscribe, signed; bulk and transactional kept apart
Moving between servers Possible with care; no standard No import yet (#734)

sections.title: Keeping this table honest
sections.html: The REST Mail column is only true at the commit this guide was built from. Each linked issue says what "done" means; when one closes, the row changes. If you find a problem this guide does not cover, or a claim it gets wrong, please open an issue.

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.part: Reference
chapters.summary: Every term this guide uses, in a sentence, with the chapter that explains it.
chapters.intro:
ARC (Authenticated Received Chain). Header fields with which a forwarder or mailing list records, and signs, the authentication results it saw. ARC.

Alignment. DMARC's requirement that the domain that passed SPF or DKIM match the From: domain. DMARC.

Autoconfig. A file a mail provider publishes so mail apps can find its servers. Finding the server.

Autodiscover. Microsoft's equivalent of autoconfig, used by Outlook. Finding the server.

Backscatter. Bounces sent to the forged sender of spam, an innocent party. Bounces.

Bcc. A recipient who appears only in the envelope, never in the header. The message itself.

BIMI. A way for a domain with DMARC at enforcement to publish a logo for mail apps to show. Efforts to modernise email.

Blocklist (DNSBL). A DNS-published list of addresses known to send spam. Spam defences.

Bounce (DSN). A message telling the sender that delivery failed. Bounces.

Canonicalization. How a message is normalised before DKIM hashes it: simple or relaxed. DKIM.

DANE. Publishing a server's TLS key in DNSSEC-signed DNS, so senders can require and verify TLS. MTA-STS and DANE.

DKIM. A signature over a message, by a domain, checked with a key in the DNS. DKIM.

DMARC. A domain's policy for mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment, and its reports. DMARC.

DNSSEC. Signatures on DNS answers, so they can be checked. MTA-STS and DANE.

Envelope. The sender (MAIL FROM) and recipients (RCPT TO) given in the SMTP conversation, separate from the message. The message itself.

Greylisting. Temporarily refusing a first attempt from an unknown sender, and accepting the retry. Spam defences.

HELO / EHLO. The command that opens an SMTP conversation and names the client. SMTP.

IMAP. The protocol mail apps use to read mail kept on the server. Reading mail.

Implicit MX. Delivering to a domain's own address when it has no MX records. DNS for email.

Implicit TLS. TLS from the first byte of the connection, on ports 465, 993 and 995. Encryption in transit.

JMAP. A JSON-over-HTTPS protocol for mail apps, IMAP's modern successor. Reading mail.

LMTP. A local variant of SMTP used to hand mail to the mailbox server. The journey of a message.

MIME. The standard for messages with several parts: text, HTML, attachments. The message itself.

MTA (mail transfer agent). A server that moves mail between servers, such as Postfix or Exim. The servers compared.

MTA-STS. A policy, published over HTTPS, that a domain requires TLS to named MX servers. MTA-STS and DANE.

MUA (mail user agent). A mail app. The journey of a message.

MX record. The DNS record naming the servers that accept a domain's mail. DNS for email.

Null MX. MX 0 .: a domain that accepts no mail. DNS for email.

One-click unsubscribe. List-Unsubscribe-Post: unsubscribing with one HTTPS POST. Bulk mail.

Open relay. A server that delivers mail for anyone, to anyone. The open relay.

Opportunistic TLS. Encrypting when both sides can, without requiring it. Encryption in transit.

POP3. A protocol for downloading mail to one device. Reading mail.

PTR record (reverse DNS). A record mapping an IP address back to a name. DNS for email.

Queue. Where a server keeps mail it has not yet delivered. Bounces.

Relaying. Passing mail on to another server. The open relay.

Return path. The envelope sender: where bounces go. The message itself.

RESTMAIL. REST Mail's delivery between REST Mail servers over HTTPS. RESTMAIL.

Selector. The name under which a domain publishes one of its DKIM keys. DKIM.

Sieve. A language for mail rules that run on the server. Reading mail.

SMTP. The protocol that moves mail between servers, and from apps to servers. SMTP as a conversation.

SMTP AUTH (SASL). Signing in over SMTP. Who may send.

SPF. A DNS record listing which servers may send for a domain. SPF.

SRS. Rewriting a forwarded message's envelope sender, so SPF passes at the next hop. SPF.

STARTTLS. Upgrading an SMTP, IMAP or POP3 connection to TLS. Encryption in transit.

Submission. Sending from a mail app, with sign-in, on port 465 or 587. Who may send.

TLS-RPT. Daily reports from senders about TLS failures reaching a domain. MTA-STS and DANE.

TTL. How long a DNS record may be cached. DNS for email.

Warm-up. Raising a new server's sending volume slowly, to build reputation. Deliverability.

chapters.title: Check your own server: a checklist
chapters.part: Reference
chapters.summary: The checks to run on any mail server, in order, with the commands to run them and the chapter that explains each.
chapters.intro: Run these from a machine outside your network, unless a step says otherwise. Replace example.org with your domain, mx.example.org with your MX host, and 203.0.113.25 with its address. Each step links to the chapter that explains what a good answer looks like.

sections.title: DNS
sections.html:
• One MX, or several, each a host name with an A or AAAA record, and no CNAME. dig +short MX example.org, then dig +short A mx.example.org. (DNS for email)
  • Reverse DNS matches. dig +short -x 203.0.113.25 names the MX host, and that name's A record is the same address. (DNS for email)
  • Exactly one SPF record, within 10 lookups, ending in -all or ~all. dig +short TXT example.org | grep spf1. (SPF)
  • A DKIM key for every selector you sign with. dig +short TXT <selector>._domainkey.example.org. (DKIM)
  • A DMARC record, with rua pointing somewhere you read. dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.org. Start at p=none. (DMARC)
  • Domains that send no mail say so: v=spf1 -all, and a null MX if they receive none. (DNS for email)

sections.title: Not an open relay
sections.html:
• Relaying for a stranger is refused. swaks --server mx.example.org --from test@example.net --to someone@gmail.com is refused at RCPT TO with 454 or 554, not accepted with 250. (The open relay)
  • AUTH is not offered on port 25. The EHLO reply on port 25 has no AUTH line. (Who may send)
  • Submission requires sign-in, over TLS. On 465 (or 587 after STARTTLS), MAIL FROM before AUTH is refused with 530. (Who may send)

sections.title: Encryption
sections.html:
• Port 25 offers STARTTLS, with a valid certificate for the MX name. openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect mx.example.org:25 -servername mx.example.org -brief. (Encryption in transit)
  • Mail apps connect with implicit TLS, on 465, 993 and 995, TLS 1.2 or later. openssl s_client -connect mx.example.org:993 -brief.
  • No password is accepted in the clear on 587, 143 or 110 before STARTTLS.
  • MTA-STS, if published, matches reality. curl -s https://mta-sts.example.org/.well-known/mta-sts.txt lists every MX, and the _mta-sts TXT record's id changed when the policy last did. (MTA-STS and DANE)

sections.title: Sending
sections.html:
• A message to an account at a large provider passes everything. Open "Show original" and read Authentication-Results: spf=pass, dkim=pass, dmarc=pass. (DMARC)
  • The sending address is on no blocklist, and not on a list of home addresses. (Deliverability)
  • Signed-in users can only send as themselves, and have a sending limit. (Who may send)
  • Bulk mail has one-click unsubscribe, DKIM-signed. (Bulk mail)

sections.title: Receiving
sections.html:
• Mail to an address that does not exist is refused during the conversation with 550 5.1.1, not accepted and bounced later. (Bounces)
  • Mail that is accepted is delivered or bounced, never dropped. Know where each filter's discards and quarantines go. (The black hole)
  • Bounces and auto-replies are sent from <>, and never sent in reply to <>. (Bounces)

sections.title: Keeping it working
sections.html:
• The queue is not growing. postqueue -p or your server's equivalent; read the errors. (Bounces)
  • Certificates renew, for the MX, submission, IMAP, mta-sts. and autoconfig..
  • DKIM keys rotate, at least every six months. (DKIM)
  • Someone reads the DMARC and TLS-RPT reports, or software does. (Why the security layers are so hard)

sections.title: With REST Mail
sections.html: chore dns:show prints every record a domain needs, and chore dns:check compares them with what is published. The relay, sign-in, encryption, sender and refusal checks above are REST Mail's defaults, not settings; the list in Solved, solving, still open shows the gaps that remain.
